Chapter 3 Constitutive equations

3.2 Hooke's law in space

The tension test of section 3.1 gave us two numbers for every material, Young's modulus \(E\) (definition 3.1) and Poisson's ratio \(\nu\) (definition 3.8), for steel \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}3\) (BOWER, Table 3.1, PDF p. 100). But the test knows only one stress, the stress along the bar. At a point of a body the stress is described by six numbers, three normal and three shear stress components (definition 2.27 and theorem 2.41 on the symmetry of stress). The strain is described by six numbers as well, the components of the small strain tensor (definition 1.121). Our examples have shown all kinds. The sheared cube of section 1.6.2 had only a shear strain, in still water all three normal stresses are equal (section 2.6.6), and in the hanging bar a single stress comes with three normal strains. The question of this section is: how do all six strain components at a point depend on all six stress components at the same point?

We will build the answer from tension tests alone, without new measurements. First we say for what kind of material the answer will hold. Then we look at what the tension test says about all six strain components, and on the way we see what it means that a material is the same in all directions. Beside it we look at a piece that cannot widen, and at four special states that we will meet throughout the book. Next we add three tensions in three directions and get from this the response to an even pressure. Pure shear we split into a tension and a compression along the diagonals. Together this gives the relation between stresses and strains, which we test on the hanging bar. At the end we look at how the relation splits into a part that changes the volume and a part that changes the shape, and where it stops holding.

3.2.1 The model and its assumptions

We look at a small piece of material around a point \(P\) inside a body. We choose a rectangular Cartesian coordinate system with the axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). The stress at \(P\) is described by the stress components \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), ..., \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\), where \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ab}}\) is the component \(b\) of the traction vector on the face with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{a}}\): \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is on the face with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and points in the direction of the axis \(y\). By theorem 2.41 on the symmetry of stress, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\), so only six of them are different. The strain of the material close to \(P\) is described by the components of the small strain tensor ((1.59)),

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \frac12\left(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\right)\]

and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) built in the same way. The normal components measure by what fraction the lengths of the edges of a small cube change, the shear components half the change of the right angle between two edges. Here too \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\). We look for a rule whose input is the six stress components at \(P\) and whose output is the six strain components at \(P\). Such a rule for a given material is called a constitutive equation (konstitutivna enačba), hence the name of the chapter.

We will derive the rule for a material for which these assumptions hold.

  1. Elasticity. The strain close to \(P\) depends only on the stress at \(P\) at this moment, not on the stress elsewhere, and not on how fast and along which path the material was loaded. Without stress there is no strain: we measure strains from the state before loading, in which the material carries no stress. Most materials behave like this in the tension test as long as the stresses are small enough (BOWER §3.2.1, PDF p. 96). The stresses must therefore stay below the yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) (definition 2.7), above which the material deforms permanently. Then the strain is not zero even without stress: our steel, stretched to the strain \(0{,}002\) and unloaded, keeps a permanent strain of \(0{,}000878\).
  2. Linearity. Definition 3.9 requires stress and strain to be proportional in the tension test. For loading in several directions we extend this as follows. If the stress state \(A\) causes the strains \(a\) and the stress state \(B\) the strains \(b\), then both states together cause the strains \(a + b\), and \(c\) times the state \(A\) causes \(c\) times the strains \(a\), for every number \(c\), also a negative one. We add states by adding their corresponding stress components, which means that the forces on each face of the piece add up. That it also holds when the material is loaded in several directions at once is an assumption of the model, confirmed by tests for many materials at small strains (SADD §4.1-4.2, PDF p. 91). With it we will build complicated stress states from simple ones. Without it we could not build the response to several stresses at once from tension tests (section 3.2.4), and every combination of stresses would have to be measured separately. Above the yield stress it does not hold: in our steel \(100\) MPa gives the strain \(0{,}000510\), twice the stress, \(200\) MPa, gives twice the strain, \(0{,}00102\), but at \(220\) MPa the strain may already be \(0{,}002\) instead of \(0{,}00112\).
  3. Isotropy. Definition 3.10 requires that bars cut in different directions give the same \(E\) and \(\nu\) in the tension test. For loading in several directions we extend this as follows: the rule that gives the strain components from the stress components is the same in every rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, with the same two numbers \(E\) and \(\nu\), however the axes are turned (SADD §4.2, PDF p. 92, CM §6.3.5, PDF p. 266). Most metals and many plastics behave like this, because the tiny crystals and grains they consist of point in random directions (SADD, PDF p. 92). Wood and materials reinforced with fibres are not isotropic. The strip of carbon fibres in epoxy resin of section 3.4.7 has the modulus \(205\) GPa along the fibres but \(10\) GPa across them, \(20{,}5\) times less (SADD Table 11.2, PDF p. 341), so at the same stress the strip across the fibres stretches \(20{,}5\) times more. We will use isotropy in several proofs, essentially in lemmas 3.12 and 3.16, and say each time where.
  4. Small strains and small rotations. All nine partial derivatives \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x\), \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y\), ..., \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z\) are smaller in size than about \(0{,}001\). Then the small strain tensor describes the changes of lengths and right angles well (section 1.17). Also the stress computed per area before loading and the stress computed per area after loading differ for steel by less than \(0{,}2\) %, in a steel bar in a tension test by only \(0{,}039\) % (section 2.13.6), so we do not distinguish them (section 2.13). For a large rotation the small strain tensor shows a strain even where no length changes, as for the rigid rotation in section 1.17, and the rule we will derive no longer holds there (BOWER §3.2.2, PDF p. 97). For a rigid rotation by \(0{,}057^\circ\) this false strain is only \(-5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\), but for a rotation by \(2{,}6^\circ\) it is already \(-0{,}001\), nearly as much as the whole elastic strain of our steel up to the yield stress, \(220/196\,000 = 0{,}00112\) (section 1.17.6).
  5. Constant temperature. A heated material expands even without stress. The assumption is not a small correction: heated by \(10\) K, the steel of our examples stretches in all directions by \(1{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4}\), as much as a bar under the stress \(196\ \text{GPa} \cdot 1{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4} = 29{,}4\) MPa along its axis. The rule of this section therefore holds only as long as the temperature does not change. How to add a change of temperature we will see in section 3.3.

We do not need homogeneity (definition 3.11). A non-homogeneous piece is drawn, for example a piece of alloy with modulus \(E_1\) on the left and a piece with modulus \(E_2\) on the right. The rule holds at point \(P_1\) with its \(E_1\) and \(\nu_1\) and at point \(P_2\) with its \(E_2\) and \(\nu_2\). In our examples the steel is homogeneous, all the numbers are the same everywhere.

Why grains pointing in random directions give an isotropic material is shown in figure 3.47. A piece of metal consists of grains, tiny crystals. In each of them the atoms are stacked in straight rows, which we draw as thin lines, and in each grain the rows lie in another direction. A single crystal is not the same in all directions (BOWER, PDF p. 103): it resists differently along the rows than at a slant to them. Let us cut out of the piece a bar along it and a bar at a slant. Each holds many grains of all directions, so the differences between the grains average out equally in both bars and the tension test gives the same \(E\) and \(\nu\) for both. On the right is a material with fibres that all lie in the same direction, as in wood. The bar along the fibres is pulled along them, the slanted bar at a slant to them, so they give different moduli: wood is stiffer along the grain than across it (BOWER, PDF p. 103). This also shows where the assumption ends. It does not hold for a piece so small that it holds only a few grains, nor for a metal whose grains got a preferred direction during processing (BOWER, PDF p. 103).

3.2.2 Tension in one direction

Let us start with the stress we know from the tension test. In a bar pulled by an axial force the only nonzero stress component is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma\), if the axis \(x\) lies along the bar (section 2.6.6). Such a state is called uniaxial stress (enoosna napetost). The tension test gives two of the six strain components. By the definition of Young's modulus the strain along the bar is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma/E\), and by the definition of Poisson's ratio the lateral strain is \(-\nu\) times this, \(-\nu\,\sigma/E\). Two questions remain. Does the bar get thinner in the direction of the axis \(y\) by as much as in the direction of the axis \(z\)? Are the shear strains really zero, or does one of the right angles between fibres along the axes change after all? The test measures only the change of length and thickness, so it does not answer these questions. In a material that is not the same in all directions, for example a plate with fibres pulled at a slant to the fibres, the right angles do change (CM, Fig. 6.3.4, PDF pp. 267-268). The answer comes from isotropy.

Figure 3.48 shows the idea. We pull a cube of the material in the direction of the axis \(x\). Let us watch two fibres in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\), along the diagonals with the unit vectors \(\vek n_1 = (1, 1, 0)/\sqrt2\) and \(\vek n_2 = (1, -1, 0)/\sqrt2\). By (1.61) their strains are

\[\varepsilon(\vek n_1) \approx \tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} , \qquad \varepsilon(\vek n_2) \approx \tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} .\]

Suppose that \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} > 0\). The deformed cube is drawn in orange, its outline before loading grey dashed. Then the fibre along \(\vek n_1\) would stretch more than the fibre along \(\vek n_2\) (figure 3.48, middle). Now we turn the cube together with the forces by half a turn about the axis \(x\). The forces on the left and right faces still pull in the direction of the axis \(x\), so the loading is the same as before. The material is the same in all directions, so the turned cube is the same test, and again the fibre along \(\vek n_1\) would have to stretch more. But the turn has carried the more stretched fibre from the direction \(\vek n_1\) to the direction \(\vek n_2\) (figure 3.48, right). The same test cannot have two different outcomes, so \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\). Every turn that leaves the loading unchanged gives such a condition. We write this precisely with the components in turned axes, which we met in section 2.9.

The half turn does not say whether the bar gets thinner in the direction of the axis \(y\) by as much as in the direction of the axis \(z\). For that we need a quarter turn. Let us look at the cube from the direction of the axis \(x\), so that the axis \(x\) points towards us and the tension \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is perpendicular to the page (figure 3.49). We see the square cross section with the fibre along the axis \(y\), which we draw in blue, and the fibre along the axis \(z\), which we draw in blackwhite. Suppose the cross section shrank more in the direction \(y\) than in the direction \(z\) and that \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} > 0\) (middle). The orange cross section is smaller than the outline before loading, the blue fibre is shorter than the blackwhite one, and one diagonal is longer than the other. Now we turn the cube together with the forces by a quarter turn about the axis \(x\). The tension lies along the axis of the turn, so the loading does not change. After the turn (right), however, the more shrunk blue fibre lies along the axis \(z\), the less shrunk blackwhite one along the axis \(y\), and the longer diagonal points the other way. The same test would again have two different outcomes. The two fibres must therefore shrink equally, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), and the two diagonals must stay equally long, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\).

Lemma 3.12 Uniaxial stress in an isotropic material (enoosna napetost v izotropnem materialu)

Let the material at the point \(P\) satisfy assumptions 1 to 5 of section 3.2.1, with Young's modulus \(E\) and Poisson's ratio \(\nu\). Let the only nonzero stress component at the point \(P\) in some rectangular Cartesian coordinate system be \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma\). Then the strain components at \(P\) in this system are

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{\sigma}{E} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\nu\,\frac{\sigma}{E} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0 . \tag{3.15}\]
Proof

We take the components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) from the tension test and get the others with two turns about the axis \(x\), a half turn and a quarter turn, that leave the loading unchanged.

  1. In the bar of the tension test the only nonzero stress component is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) (section 2.6.6). By definition 3.1 the strain of the bar along its axis is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma/E\). By assumption 1 (elasticity) the strain close to a point depends only on the stress there, so the same holds at \(P\). For compression, \(\sigma < 0\), the same follows by assumption 2 (linearity) with the factor \(-1\).
  2. By definition 3.8 the lateral strain is \(-\nu\) times the strain along the bar. For the lateral direction \(y\) we therefore have \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -\nu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -\nu\,\sigma/E\).
  3. Take new axes with the unit vectors \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} = -\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = -\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), that is, axes turned by half a turn about the axis \(x\). By definition 2.44 the rows of the rotation matrix are the components of these vectors in the old axes, so \(\mat Q\) is diagonal with the entries \(Q_{\mathrm{xx}} = 1\), \(Q_{\mathrm{yy}} = -1\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{zz}} = -1\).
  4. By theorem 2.53 on the transformation of stress components, the stress components in the new axes are \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}}\), where the indices \(i\) and \(j\) run over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) ((2.59)). Since \(\mat Q\) is diagonal, \(Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\) is nonzero only for \(i = k\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{lj}}\) only for \(j = l\), so a single term remains, \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}} = Q_{\mathrm{kk}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}\,Q_{\mathrm{ll}}\). The only nonzero component is \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 1 \cdot \sigma \cdot 1 = \sigma\). In the new axes the stress has the same components as in the old ones: the forces after the turn pull as before it.
  5. By lemma 2.55 on the transformation of strain components the same rule holds for strains, \(\bar{\ten\varepsilon} = \mat Q\,\ten\varepsilon\,\mat Q^\T\), and by the same argument as in step 4, \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}} = Q_{\mathrm{kk}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}}\,Q_{\mathrm{ll}}\). Therefore \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 1 \cdot \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} \cdot (-1) = -\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = -\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\). The sign changes because the turn carries the more stretched diagonal to the other direction.
  6. Here we use isotropy (assumption 3): the middle and the right side of the figure are the same test. The rule that gives the strain components from the stress components is the same in the new axes as in the old ones. By step 4 the stress components in the new axes are the same numbers as in the old ones, so the strain components in the new axes are also the same numbers as in the old ones: \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\). With step 5, \(-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), so \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), and likewise \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0\).
  7. Now take the axes turned by a quarter turn about the axis \(x\): \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = -\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). The rows of the rotation matrix are \((1, 0, 0)\), \((0, 0, 1)\) and \((0, -1, 0)\). Each row has a single nonzero entry: \(Q_{\mathrm{xx}} = 1\), \(Q_{\mathrm{yz}} = 1\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{zy}} = -1\).
  8. In the sum of step 4, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is nonzero only for \(i = j = x\), so \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}} = Q_{\mathrm{kx}}\,\sigma\,Q_{\mathrm{lx}}\). The entry \(Q_{\mathrm{kx}}\) is nonzero only for \(k = x\), so again the only nonzero component is \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma\), the tension along the axis of the turn.
  9. By the lemma on the transformation of strain components, \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{yi}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{yj}}\). In the row \(y\) only \(Q_{\mathrm{yz}} = 1\) is nonzero, so \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\): the turn puts the fibre along the axis \(y\) along the axis \(z\). Likewise \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = Q_{\mathrm{yz}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zy}}\,Q_{\mathrm{zy}} = -\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zy}} = -\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\), since the small strain tensor is symmetric.
  10. Again we use isotropy as in step 6, the middle and the right side of the figure are the same test: \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\). Therefore \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -\nu\,\sigma/E\) and \(-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\), so \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\).

Source: SADD §4.3.1 (PDF p. 95), CM (6.3.40) (PDF p. 267). The sources read the result off the general law for an isotropic material (SADD (4.2.10), PDF p. 93), which we are only building here. The argument with turns is not from the sources.

The proof has shown what isotropy demands of a material. A turn that leaves the loading unchanged must not change the strain either. The strain components whose sign such a turn reverses must therefore be zero, and the components that the turn exchanges must be equal. For a bar pulled along the axis \(x\) such turns are the half turn and the quarter turn about this axis. In steel with \(\nu = 0{,}3\) a piece that gets longer by a thousandth along the axis \(x\) gets shorter by \(0{,}3\) thousandths in all lateral directions, and the right angles between fibres along the axes stay right.

3.2.3 A piece that cannot widen

In the tension test the side faces of the bar are free. What if something holds them? Such is a piece of material in a tight hole, a thin layer between two thick plates, or material in the middle of a thick wall, which the neighbouring material does not let widen. Does Young's modulus \(E\) describe such a piece too? No, and the reason is Poisson's ratio.

Take a steel cube with the edge 50 mm and put it on a smooth rigid base (figure 3.50, left). The axis \(x\) points up, the axis \(y\) to the right, the axis \(z\) towards us. We press on the top face with an even pressure \(p = 127{,}3\) MPa, as large as the stress in the bar of section 3.1.2. The side faces are free, so this is uniaxial stress with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = -p\). By lemma 3.12 on uniaxial stress,

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -\frac{p}{E} = -6{,}496 \cdot 10^{-4} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \nu\,\frac{p}{E} = 1{,}949 \cdot 10^{-4} .\]

The cube gets lower by \(6{,}496 \cdot 10^{-4} \cdot 50\ \text{mm} = 32{,}48\) µm and wider by \(1{,}949 \cdot 10^{-4} \cdot 50\ \text{mm} = 9{,}74\) µm, by \(4{,}87\) µm on each side. In the figure the changes are magnified about nine thousand times, all on the same scale.

Now we put the same cube into a die, a hole with rigid smooth walls that it just fits (figure 3.50, right), and press with the same pressure \(p\). The cube would like to widen by \(9{,}74\) µm, but the walls do not allow it. What happens we see in four steps, shown by the middle part of the figure.

  1. First we think the walls away. The cube gets lower and wider as on the left. In the middle this state is drawn orange dashed.
  2. Then we squeeze the cube from the sides back to its old width. We press on each of the four side faces with a pressure \(q\). The pressure \(q\) in the direction \(y\) narrows the cube in this direction by \(q/E\), and the pressure \(q\) in the direction \(z\) widens it in the direction \(y\) by \(\nu\,q/E\), by the definition of Poisson's ratio. Together it narrows in the direction \(y\) by \((1 - \nu)\,q/E\). This must cancel the widening \(\nu\,p/E\) of the first step:
    \[(1 - \nu)\,\frac{q}{E} = \nu\,\frac{p}{E} , \qquad q = \frac{\nu}{1 - \nu}\,p = \frac{0{,}3}{0{,}7} \cdot 127{,}32\ \text{MPa} = 54{,}57\ \text{MPa} .\]
  3. But squeezing from the sides also makes the cube higher. Each of the two side pressures lengthens it in the direction \(x\) by \(\nu\,q/E\), both together by
    \[2\nu\,\frac{q}{E} = \frac{2 \cdot 0{,}3 \cdot 54{,}57\ \text{MPa}}{196\,000\ \text{MPa}} = 1{,}670 \cdot 10^{-4} ,\]
    which on the edge of 50 mm is \(8{,}35\) µm.
  4. In the die the cube therefore gets lower by only \(32{,}48 - 8{,}35 = 24{,}13\) µm. On the right it is drawn in orange below the dashed line of its former height. The walls press on it with the pressure \(q = 54{,}57\) MPa, although we pressed only from above.

We may add because of linearity (assumption 2), and exchange the roles of the axes because of isotropy (assumption 3). The strain of the cube in the die is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -24{,}13\ \mu\text{m}/50\ \text{mm} = -4{,}826 \cdot 10^{-4}\), and all other components are zero. The quotient of stress and strain along the axis \(x\) is

\[\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}} = \frac{-127{,}3\ \text{MPa}}{-4{,}826 \cdot 10^{-4}} = 263{,}8\ \text{GPa} ,\]

which is \(1{,}346\) times \(E = 196\) GPa. A piece that cannot widen is therefore a good third stiffer than a free bar of the same material. The material is the same. The difference is in the walls: while they hold the cube at its width, they also lengthen it against the pressure from above.

We idealized the die twice. Figure 3.51 shows how much each idealization changes the outcome. First, the walls are rigid. A real wall also gives way under the pressure \(q\) and the cube widens a little. The horizontal axis of the left graph shows how much the cube widens, from \(0\) to the free widening of \(9{,}74\) µm, and the vertical one the quotient \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) in units of \(E\). The curve runs from \(1{,}346\,E\) for rigid walls to \(E\) for free faces, and the real quotient lies between them. Suppose the walls allow a tenth of the free widening, \(0{,}97\) µm. Then the walls must squeeze the cube back by only nine tenths of the widening, so the side pressure in step 2 is only \(0{,}9\,q\) and the rise of step 3 only \(0{,}9 \cdot 8{,}35 = 7{,}52\) µm. The cube gets lower by \(32{,}48 - 7{,}52 = 24{,}96\) µm, and the quotient is

\[\frac{127{,}3\ \text{MPa}}{24{,}96\ \mu\text{m}/50\ \text{mm}} = 255{,}0\ \text{GPa} = 1{,}301\,E ,\]

the dot on the curve, instead of \(1{,}346\,E\). The computation is good when the die is much stiffer than the piece, for example for a plastic in steel.

Second, the walls are smooth. If the cube slides along the walls with friction, friction carries part of the force from above, the pressure in the cube falls with depth and the state is no longer the same at all points. We estimate the share of friction on the cube in the middle of figure 3.51. Under the pressure \(p\) the cube gets lower, so its side faces slide down along the walls and friction acts on them upwards. Suppose friction acts on a face of the cube with at most a tenth of the pressure with which the wall presses on it. The four walls press on four faces, each as large as the top one, and with at most the pressure \(q = 54{,}57\) MPa, since the pressure falls with depth. On top we press with \(p = 127{,}3\) MPa on a single face. On the right the two forces are drawn as bars in units of MPa times the area of one face: the force from above \(127{,}3\) and the largest friction force \(4 \cdot 0{,}1 \cdot 54{,}57 = 21{,}83\). Friction therefore carries at most \(21{,}83/127{,}3 = 0{,}17\) of the force from above.

The state we have found has a name.

Definition 3.13 Uniaxial strain (enoosno deformacijsko stanje)

The strain at a point \(P\) of a body is uniaxial strain (enoosno deformacijsko stanje) if there is a rectangular Cartesian coordinate system in which the only nonzero component of the small strain tensor at \(P\) is the component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\):

\[\ten\varepsilon = \begin{bmatrix} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The name says that the material stretches or shrinks along a single axis. The uniaxial stress of lemma 3.12, where a stress acts along a single axis, is also called the state of uniaxial stress. In the free cube the stress is uniaxial and the strain is not. In the cube in the die the strain is uniaxial and the stress is not.

Lemma 3.14 Stress in uniaxial strain (napetost pri enoosni deformaciji)

Let the material at the point \(P\) satisfy assumptions 1 to 5 of section 3.2.1, with Young's modulus \(E\) and Poisson's ratio \(\nu \neq 1\). In some rectangular Cartesian coordinate system let the stress components at \(P\) be

\[\ten\sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & q & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & q \end{bmatrix} , \qquad q = \frac{\nu}{1 - \nu}\,\sigma . \tag{3.16}\]

Then the strain at \(P\) is uniaxial strain with the components

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{(1 + \nu)(1 - 2\nu)}{(1 - \nu)\,E}\,\sigma , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0 . \tag{3.17}\]

If in addition \(\nu \neq -1\) and \(\nu \neq \tfrac12\), then

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{(1 - \nu)\,E}{(1 + \nu)(1 - 2\nu)}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \frac{\nu\,E}{(1 + \nu)(1 - 2\nu)}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{\nu}{1 - \nu}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} . \tag{3.18}\]
Proof

We split the stress into three uniaxial stresses and add their strains by linearity, as we did with numbers in figure 3.50. There \(\sigma = -p\), and the side stress of the lemma is \(-q\) of the figure.

Figure 3.52 shows the proof with the numbers of the cube in the die, \(\sigma = -127{,}32\) MPa and \(q = -54{,}57\) MPa. At the top are three cubes, each with one pair of pressures: the first from above and below, the second from left and right in the direction of the axis \(y\), the third from the front and the back in the direction of the axis \(z\). Beside the second and the third cube the new names of the axes are written in grey, with which the pressure lies along the first axis \(\bar x\). At the bottom are three vertical lines for \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) in units of \(10^{-4}\), all with the zero at the same height. On each line three arrows follow one another, the contributions of the first, the second and the third cube. Each arrow starts where the previous one ends, so the orange dot at the end of the last one is the sum of all three.

  1. We write the stress matrix as a sum of three matrices, added entry by entry:
    \[\ten\sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & q & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & q \end{bmatrix} .\]
    The first is the pressure from above, the second and the third are the pressures on the side faces in the directions \(y\) and \(z\).
  2. The first matrix is uniaxial stress along the axis \(x\). By lemma 3.12 on uniaxial stress it causes \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma/E\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\nu\,\sigma/E\) and no shear strain. This is the free cube. In figure 3.52 these are the first arrows, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -6{,}496\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 1{,}949\) (in units of \(10^{-4}\)).
  3. The lemma on uniaxial stress holds in every rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, since by assumption 3 (isotropy) the rule is the same in all of them. If we rename the axis \(y\) to \(x\), the axis \(z\) to \(y\) and the axis \(x\) to \(z\), the second matrix becomes a uniaxial stress \(q\) along the first axis. In the old axes it therefore causes \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = q/E\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -\nu\,q/E\) and no shear strain. This is the pressure of the walls in the direction \(y\), which makes the cube narrower and higher. In figure 3.52 these are the second arrows, \(-2{,}784\) on the line \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(0{,}835\) on the other two.
  4. If we rename the axis \(z\) to \(x\), the axis \(x\) to \(y\) and the axis \(y\) to \(z\), the third matrix becomes a uniaxial stress \(q\) along the first axis. In the old axes it therefore causes \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = q/E\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -\nu\,q/E\) and no shear strain. This is the pressure on the two side faces that in the figure face towards us and away from us. In figure 3.52 these are the third arrows, \(-2{,}784\) on the line \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) and \(0{,}835\) on the other two.
  5. By assumption 2 (linearity) the strains are the sums of the strains of steps 2 to 4. The shear strains are zero, and the normal strains are
    \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{\sigma - 2\nu\,q}{E} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \frac{q - \nu\,(\sigma + q)}{E} = \frac{(1 - \nu)\,q - \nu\,\sigma}{E} .\]
    The term \(-2\nu\,q/E\) is the rise caused by the walls. With numbers, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -6{,}496 + 0{,}835 + 0{,}835 = -4{,}826\) (in units of \(10^{-4}\)).
  6. We insert \(q = \nu\,\sigma/(1 - \nu)\). Then \((1 - \nu)\,q = \nu\,\sigma\), so \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\): the side pressure brings the cube back to its old width. In figure 3.52 the second and the third arrow on the line \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) together measure \(-2{,}784 + 0{,}835 = -1{,}949\) and cancel the first, so the sum is zero.
  7. We insert the same \(q\) into \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and put both terms over a common denominator:
    \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{\sigma}{E}\left(1 - \frac{2\nu^2}{1 - \nu}\right) = \frac{\sigma}{E} \cdot \frac{1 - \nu - 2\nu^2}{1 - \nu} .\]
  1. We factor the numerator, since \((1 + \nu)(1 - 2\nu) = 1 - 2\nu + \nu - 2\nu^2 = 1 - \nu - 2\nu^2\). This gives (3.17).
  2. If \(\nu \neq -1\) and \(\nu \neq \tfrac12\), the factor in front of \(\sigma\) in (3.17) is not zero and we solve the equation for \(\sigma = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\). From \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = q = \nu\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/(1 - \nu)\) the second part of (3.18) follows.

Source: The result follows from the law for an isotropic material, CM (6.3.32) (PDF p. 266) and SADD (4.2.7) (PDF p. 93), with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\). CM (PDF p. 309) writes \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = (2\mu + \lambda)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) for the beam, where it then takes \(\nu = 0\), so that the factor equals \(E\). The derivation by adding three uniaxial stresses and the example with the die are not from the sources.

The lemma goes from stress to strain, because that is how we add tensions. That this is the only stress that gives uniaxial strain will follow in section 3.2.9, where we turn the rule around. There the two combinations of the numbers \(E\) and \(\nu\) in (3.18) will get names. The second will be the constant \(\lambda\), and the first \(\lambda + 2\mu\), where \(\mu\) will be one more combination of the same two numbers. Uniaxial strain is then written briefly, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = (\lambda + 2\mu)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\). For the cube in the die, \(\lambda + 2\mu = 263{,}8\) GPa and \(\lambda = 113{,}1\) GPa, and indeed \(113{,}08\ \text{GPa} \cdot 4{,}826 \cdot 10^{-4} = 54{,}57\) MPa, the pressure of the walls. In the lectures the axes are numbered, so there one writes \(\sigma_{11} = (2\mu + \lambda)\,\varepsilon_{11}\) and \(\sigma_{22} = \sigma_{33} = \lambda\,\varepsilon_{11}\).

How much stiffer the held piece is and how hard it presses on the walls depends only on Poisson's ratio. The table shows the two factors of (3.18) for materials from the table in section 3.1.8.

material \(\nu\) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/(E\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}})\) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}/\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\)
no lateral contraction 0 1 0
silica glass 0,16 1,065 0,190
steel 0,30 1,346 0,429
aluminium 0,35 1,605 0,538
natural rubber 0,49 17,11 0,961

Figure 3.53 shows both columns of the table as curves. The horizontal axes carry \(\nu\) from \(0\) to \(0{,}5\). On the left is the stiffness factor \((1 - \nu)/\bigl((1 + \nu)(1 - 2\nu)\bigr)\), on the right the ratio of the side stress \(\nu/(1 - \nu)\), and the dots are the materials of the table. As \(\nu\) approaches the dashed vertical line at \(0{,}5\), \(1 - 2\nu\) in the denominator of the left factor goes to zero, so the factor grows beyond all bounds. The right factor meanwhile approaches \(0{,}5/0{,}5 = 1\).

A material with \(\nu = 0\) does not widen when compressed, so it does not feel the walls and is as stiff as when free. The closer \(\nu\) is to one half, the more the piece wants to widen, the harder the walls must hold it and the stiffer it is. Rubber is soft as a bar, but in a die it is seventeen times stiffer, and it presses on the walls with nearly the same pressure with which we press on it. This is the reason why \(E\) is not the stiffness of a piece held at its sides. In chapter 5 we will use this for a fibre of a beam, which has free side faces and therefore the stiffness \(E\), not \(1{,}346\,E\).

Uniaxial stress and uniaxial strain are two of four special states that we will meet throughout the book. Figure 3.54 puts them into one pattern. For each state the stress matrix is drawn at the top and the strain matrix at the bottom. A cell is blue if the component is given and not zero, grey if it is given as zero, and orange if it follows from the material. A whiteblack cell is an unknown that only the problem determines.

  1. Uniaxial stress is state (1). The whole stress matrix is given, one component and five zeros. All strains are the outcome: three normal ones by (3.15) and three shear zeros. The example is the bar in the tension test.
  2. Uniaxial strain is state (2), the mirror image of the first. The whole strain matrix is given, all stresses are the outcome by (3.18). The example is the cube in the die.
  3. Plane stress (ravninsko napetostno stanje) is state (3). Three zeros in the stress matrix are given: there is no stress on the face with the normal along the axis \(z\). The example is a thin plate with free faces, loaded in its own plane. The components in the plane \(x\), \(y\) are neither given nor an outcome, they are the unknowns of the problem. The outcome is two shear zeros and the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), by which the plate gets thinner or thicker.
  4. Plane strain (ravninsko deformacijsko stanje) is state (4), the mirror image of the third. Three zeros in the strain matrix are given, because a long body cannot stretch along the axis \(z\). The components in the plane are the unknowns of the problem. The outcome is two shear zeros and the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\), with which the body keeps its length, just as the walls of the die keep the width of the cube.

We will compute the orange cells of the states (3) and (4) when we have the law for all components (section 3.2.9), and define the two states precisely in section 11.9. The pattern holds already now: where something prevents a strain of the body, a stress appears that would otherwise not be there, and where a face is free, a strain appears.

3.2.4 Three tensions at once

What if we pull the piece in the directions of all three axes at once, with different stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\), and there are no shear stress components? Such a state is the sum of three uniaxial stresses, and by linearity we add their strains (figure 3.55). The axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) point in the figure towards us, to the right and up.

  1. We split the state into three. In the first the only nonzero stress component is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), in the second \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\), in the third \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\). The sum of the corresponding components of all three is the given state.
  2. By lemma 3.12 on uniaxial stress the first state gives the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\nu\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E\) and no shear strains.
  3. The lemma holds in every rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, and we choose the names of the axes ourselves. If we rename the axis \(y\) to \(x\), the axis \(z\) to \(y\) and the axis \(x\) to \(z\), the only nonzero stress component of the second state is the one along the first axis. The second state therefore gives \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}/E\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -\nu\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}/E\) and no shear strains.
  4. In the same way the third state gives \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}/E\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -\nu\,\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}/E\) and no shear strains.
  5. By linearity we add the strains of all three states. The component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) receives \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E\) from the first state, \(-\nu\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}/E\) from the second and \(-\nu\,\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}/E\) from the third, and likewise the other two:
    \[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} &= \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \nu\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}})}{E} , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} &= \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} - \nu\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}})}{E} , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} &= \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} - \nu\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}})}{E} . \end{aligned} \tag{3.19}\]
    The shear strains are sums of zeros, so they are zero.

Each tension stretches the material in its own direction and makes it thinner in the other two, when \(\nu > 0\). A second tension in a lateral direction therefore reduces the lengthening in the direction of the first. Let us try it with numbers on a steel cube with the modulus of elasticity \(E = 196\) GPa and Poisson's ratio \(\nu = 0{,}3\) (figure 3.56). We look at it from above, the axis \(x\) points to the right, the axis \(y\) up, the axis \(z\) towards us. We draw the cube before loading grey and dashed, its edge measures \(10\) mm.

First we pull it with the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 100\) MPa in one direction only. By (3.19),

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{100 \cdot 10^6\ \text{Pa}}{196 \cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa}} = 5{,}102 \cdot 10^{-4} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -0{,}3 \cdot 5{,}102 \cdot 10^{-4} = -1{,}531 \cdot 10^{-4} .\]

The edge along the axis \(x\) gets longer by \(5{,}102 \cdot 10^{-4} \cdot 10\ \text{mm} = 5{,}102\) µm, the edge along the axis \(y\) gets shorter by \(1{,}531\) µm.

Now we also pull it with the same stress in the direction of the axis \(y\). By (3.19),

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{(100 - 0{,}3 \cdot 100) \cdot 10^6\ \text{Pa}}{196 \cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa}} = 3{,}571 \cdot 10^{-4} ,\]

\(30\) % less than before, because the tension in the direction of the axis \(y\) makes the cube thinner in the direction of the axis \(x\) by \(0{,}3\) times its own strain. The edge along the axis \(x\) now gets longer by only \(3{,}571\) µm, and the edge along the axis \(y\) by the same, since the two stresses are equal. In the direction of the axis \(z\), which points towards us and in which the cube is not pulled, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -0{,}3 \cdot (100 + 100) \cdot 10^6\ \text{Pa}/(196 \cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa}) = -3{,}061 \cdot 10^{-4}\). The edge along the axis \(z\) gets shorter by \(3{,}061\) µm, because both tensions make it thinner, just as the first cube of figure 3.55 gets thinner in both directions in which it is not pulled.

In figure 3.55 the stresses are in the ratio \(3 : 2 : 1\), and the edge along the axis \(z\) gets shorter although it is pulled: its own tension lengthens it by \(1\) part, the tensions in the other two directions shorten it by \(0{,}3 \cdot (3 + 2) = 1{,}5\) parts.

3.2.5 Even pressure and the bulk modulus

In still water the stress at every point is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = -p\), and there are no shear components (section 2.6.6). We sink a small steel cube with the edge \(h = 10\) mm into the water. The water pushes on each of its faces perpendicularly, with the pressure \(p\). We look at it from the front, the axis \(x\) points to the right, the axis \(z\) up. We assume that the stress in the whole cube is the same too, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = -p\) without shear components. This state agrees with the forces of the water on all six faces, since by Cauchy's formula the traction vector on a face with the outward normal \(\vek n\) is \(-p\,\vek n\), exactly the force of the water per unit area. It also satisfies the equilibrium equations of section 2.7, since its components do not change from point to point if we neglect the weight of the cube. The weight of the cube, with the density of steel \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m³ (BOWER, Table 3.1, PDF p. 100), changes the stress between its top and bottom, which are \(h\) apart, by \(\rho g h = 7800\ \text{kg/m}^3 \cdot 9{,}81\ \text{m/s}^2 \cdot 0{,}01\ \text{m} = 765\) Pa, which we will compare with the pressure below. By how much does the cube shrink?

  1. Into (3.19) we put the pressure on all faces, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = -p\):
    \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{-p - \nu\,(-p - p)}{E} = -\frac{(1 - 2\nu)\,p}{E} ,\]
    and likewise \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\). There are no shear strains.
  2. For \(\nu < 0{,}5\), as for steel with \(\nu = 0{,}3\), we have \(1 - 2\nu > 0\), so all edges get shorter by the same fraction. The right angles stay right, since there are no shear strains. The cube stays a cube, only smaller (figure 3.57).
  3. By how much does the volume decrease? A piece in the shape of a box with the edges \(\Delta x\), \(\Delta y\) and \(\Delta z\) along the axes, which has only normal strains and does not rotate, like our cube, has after loading the edges \((1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}})\,\Delta x\), \((1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}})\,\Delta y\) and \((1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}})\,\Delta z\), which are still perpendicular. In figure 3.57 this is the cube with the edge \(h\), which after loading has the edge \((1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}})\,h\). The volume of the piece therefore changes from \(V_0 = \Delta x\,\Delta y\,\Delta z\) to
    \[V_1 = V_0\,(1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}})(1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}})(1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}) .\]
  4. The volume of the shrunken cube is a product of three edges. What the product of the brackets gives we see when we cut the box with the edges \((1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}})\,h\), \((1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}})\,h\) and \((1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}})\,h\) into pieces (figure 3.58). The figure is drawn for the stretches \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0{,}1\), at which the pieces can be seen. The largest piece is the original cube with the volume \(V_0 = h^3\). On three of its faces lie three thin slabs with the thicknesses \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} h\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} h\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} h\) and the volumes \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} V_0\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} V_0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} V_0\). Between the slabs, along three edges, remain three rods, each thin in two directions, with the volumes \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} V_0\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} V_0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} V_0\). In the corner remains a small cube, thin in all three directions, with the volume \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} V_0\). Exactly these terms come out when we multiply out the brackets, multiplying each term of the first by each term of the second and then by the third. When the cube shrinks, the strains are negative and the slabs mean volume taken away, but the product of the brackets is the same. We subtract the original cube and divide by \(V_0\):
    \[\frac{V_1 - V_0}{V_0} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} .\]
    When the strains are smaller in size than \(0{,}001\), each product of two strains, the volume of one rod divided by \(V_0\), is smaller than \(10^{-6}\), so at least a thousand times smaller than each of the two strains, and we drop the products. This is where the assumption of small strains enters. What does it cost? For our cube below each of the three strains will be \(-2{,}002 \cdot 10^{-6}\), and the dropped products amount together to about \(3 \cdot (2{,}002 \cdot 10^{-6})^2 = 1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-11}\), two millionths of the computed change of volume. With strains of \(0{,}1\) in all three directions, however, the exact change would be \(1{,}1^3 - 1 = 0{,}331\) instead of the sum \(0{,}3\) of the three slabs. The rods and the corner add \(0{,}031\), the error is \(9\) %, and there this step must not be made. For small strains the relative change of volume is thus approximately the sum of the normal strains,
    \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} ,\]
    the volumetric strain of definition 2.114. We did the same computation already in section 1.17.4. That the same holds for a piece with shear strains is the content of lemma 2.77 on the change of volume.
  5. Under even pressure, by step 1, the relative change of the volume of the shrunken cube is therefore
    \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = -\frac{3\,(1 - 2\nu)\,p}{E} .\]

The pressure and the relative decrease of volume are thus proportional. Their ratio is a number that tells how strongly the material resists a change of volume.

Definition 3.15 Bulk modulus (modul stisljivosti)

Let a pressure \(p > 0\) act equally from all sides on a small piece of a linear elastic isotropic material, so that the stress in it is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = -p\) without shear components, let \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) be the volumetric strain that this pressure causes, and let \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} \neq 0\). The bulk modulus (modul stisljivosti) of the material is the number

\[K = \frac{p}{-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}} .\]

Source: SADD (4.3.1) (PDF p. 96), BOWER §3.2.5 (PDF p. 101).

The minus sign is there because pressure decreases the volume, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} < 0\), while the bulk modulus should be positive. In the lectures this number is called the compression modulus (kompresijski modul) and has the symbol \(k\) or \(\varkappa\), and the volumetric strain has the symbol \(e\), so that there \(k = -p/e\). The ratio does not depend on \(p\), since by step 5 \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\) is proportional to \(p\). Putting in \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\) from step 5 we get

\[K = \frac{E}{3\,(1 - 2\nu)} . \tag{3.20}\]

For steel \(K = 196\ \text{GPa}/\big(3\,(1 - 2 \cdot 0{,}3)\big) = 196\ \text{GPa}/(3 \cdot 0{,}4) = 163{,}3\) GPa, somewhat less than \(E\). BOWER notes that the bulk modulus is usually larger than Young's modulus (BOWER §3.2.6, PDF p. 102). This holds only for \(\nu > 1/3\). Let us draw the ratio \(K/E = 1/\big(3\,(1 - 2\nu)\big)\) from (3.20) as a function of Poisson's ratio \(\nu\) between \(0\) and \(0{,}5\) (figure 3.59). The curve starts at \(K/E = 1/3\) for \(\nu = 0\) and rises, because the denominator \(3\,(1 - 2\nu)\) gets smaller as \(\nu\) grows. The horizontal dashed line is \(K = E\). The curve crosses it at \(\nu = 1/3\), where \(3\,(1 - 2\nu) = 1\). For \(\nu < 0{,}5\) the denominator is positive, so the ratio is larger than \(1\) exactly when \(3\,(1 - 2\nu) < 1\), that is, to the right of the crossing, for \(\nu > 1/3\). Steel with \(\nu = 0{,}3\) lies to the left of the crossing, \(K = 0{,}833\,E\). Copper with \(\nu = 0{,}34\) (BOWER, Table 3.1, PDF p. 100) lies just to the right of it, \(K = 1{,}04\,E\). SADD too gives a bulk modulus of \(164\) GPa for steel, less than its Young's modulus of \(207\) GPa (SADD, Table 4.2, PDF p. 97).

How much does our cube shrink at a depth of 100 m (figure 3.60)? The pressure in the water there is larger by \(\rho_{\mathrm{w}} g d\) than at the surface (section 2.7), where \(\rho_{\mathrm{w}}\) is the density of water, about \(1000\) kg/m³ (VK, Appendix A.4, PDF p. 637), and \(d = 100\) m the depth of the cube:

\[p = 1000\ \text{kg/m}^3 \cdot 9{,}81\ \text{m/s}^2 \cdot 100\ \text{m} = 981\,000\ \text{Pa} = 0{,}981\ \text{MPa} .\]

At the surface the air already pushes with about \(100\) kPa (VK, Appendix A.4, PDF p. 637). By linearity an additional pressure causes an additional strain, whatever pressure acted before, so we compute only the change from the surface. The volumetric strain is

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = -\frac{p}{K} = -\frac{0{,}981 \cdot 10^6\ \text{Pa}}{163{,}33 \cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa}} = -6{,}006 \cdot 10^{-6} .\]

On the right of figure 3.60 the same cube is magnified. At the surface we draw it grey and dashed, with the edge \(10\) mm, at the depth of \(100\) m orange, and the shrinking is strongly exaggerated. The water pushes on all its faces with the pressure \(p\). The cube with the volume \(1000\) mm³ loses \(0{,}006006\) mm³. Each edge gets shorter by a third of this fraction, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}/3 = -2{,}002 \cdot 10^{-6}\), that is, by \(10\ \text{mm} \cdot 2{,}002 \cdot 10^{-6} = 2{,}002 \cdot 10^{-5}\) mm, which is \(20{,}02\) nm. A nanometre, nm, is a thousandth of a micrometre. The weight of the cube changes the stress by \(765\) Pa, which is \(0{,}08\) % of the pressure \(981\,000\) Pa. On the bottom of the cube the water pushes with a pressure larger by \(\rho_{\mathrm{w}} g h = 98{,}1\) Pa than on the top, which is \(0{,}01\) % of the pressure. We were therefore right to neglect the weight and the pressure difference.

The volume also changes under tension in one direction, where the piece gets longer in one direction and thinner in the other two. By lemma 3.12 on uniaxial stress,

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = \frac{\sigma}{E} - \nu\,\frac{\sigma}{E} - \nu\,\frac{\sigma}{E} = (1 - 2\nu)\,\frac{\sigma}{E} = (1 - 2\nu)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} .\]

A steel bar that gets longer by a thousandth increases its volume by \((1 - 2 \cdot 0{,}3) \cdot 0{,}001 = 0{,}4 \cdot 0{,}001 = 0{,}0004\), that is, by \(0{,}04\) %. The same number, up to the dropped products, we computed in section 1.6 from the thinning by \(0{,}3\) thousandths. For \(\nu = 0{,}5\), however, \(1 - 2\nu = 0\), the volume does not change for small strains (the dropped products give only \(-7{,}5 \cdot 10^{-7}\) at \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0{,}001\)), and as \(\nu\) approaches \(0{,}5\), the bulk modulus in (3.20) grows without bound. We return to this at the end of the section.

3.2.6 Pure shear and the shear modulus

The shear stress components remain. Take the pure shear of section 2.6.6. We load a cube only with forces along its faces, the axis \(x\) points to the right, the axis \(z\) up, and the corners of the front face are \(A\) at the bottom left, \(B\) at the bottom right, \(C\) at the top right and \(D\) at the top left. The only nonzero stress components are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \tau_0\). None of the lemmas so far tells us what the strain is. In section 2.9, however, we put axes along the diagonals of the front face,

\[\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\,(1, 0, 1) , \qquad \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} = (0, 1, 0) , \qquad \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\,(-1, 0, 1) ,\]

the axis \(\bar x\) from \(A\) toward \(C\) and the axis \(\bar z\) from \(B\) toward \(D\), and computed that the components of the same stress in these axes are

\[\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tau_0 , \qquad \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\tau_0 , \qquad \text{all other } \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}} = 0 .\]

On the faces perpendicular to the diagonal \(AC\) a tension \(\tau_0\) acts, on the faces perpendicular to the diagonal \(BD\) a compression \(\tau_0\), and in these axes there are no shear components. Pure shear is thus the sum of a tension \(\tau_0\) in the direction of the diagonal \(AC\) and a compression \(\tau_0\) in the direction of the diagonal \(BD\) (figure 3.61). That this is really the same state we also saw in section 2.6.6 without turning the axes, by adding forces: the triangular piece \(ABD\) that a diagonal cuts off the cube is at rest, so the forces on its bottom and left faces are balanced by the force on the diagonal face, which points perpendicular to it, that is, by a tension. For tension and compression in one direction we already know the strains. We write them in the diagonal axes and carry them back to the axes of the cube.

What will come out can be seen before any calculation (figure 3.62). Let us draw the front face of the cube, the square \(ABCD\), three times, grey and dashed, as it is before loading, and load it in three ways.

  1. Only the tension \(\tau_0\) along the diagonal \(AC\). By lemma 3.12 on uniaxial stress the material gets longer in the direction of the tension by the fraction \(\tau_0/E\), so the diagonal \(AC\) gets longer by this fraction: this is the blue distance between the old and the new corner \(C\). Across the tension the material gets thinner by \(\nu\) times as much, so the diagonal \(BD\) gets shorter by the fraction \(\nu\,\tau_0/E\). The square becomes an orange rhombus, a quadrilateral with four equal sides.
  2. Only the compression \(\tau_0\) along the diagonal \(BD\). The diagonal \(BD\) gets shorter by the fraction \(\tau_0/E\). A compressed material widens sideways, so the diagonal \(AC\) gets longer by the fraction \(\nu\,\tau_0/E\). The result is another rhombus.
  3. Both at once, which is pure shear. By linearity the changes add, as the signs between the pictures show. The diagonal \(AC\) gets longer by the fraction \(\tau_0/E + \nu\,\tau_0/E = (1 + \nu)\,\tau_0/E\), the diagonal \(BD\) gets shorter by the same fraction, and we get a third rhombus.

The factor \(1 + \nu\) thus comes from two things lengthening the diagonal \(AC\) at once: the tension along it and the compression across it. In the direction of the axis \(y\), perpendicular to the picture, the tension makes the material thinner by \(\nu\,\tau_0/E\), the compression widens it by the same amount, and nothing changes there. For steel and \(\tau_0 = 50\) MPa, \(\tau_0/E = 2{,}551 \cdot 10^{-4}\) and \((1 + \nu)\,\tau_0/E = 3{,}316 \cdot 10^{-4}\), more than a thousand times less than in the figure. The lemma says the same precisely and also shows that this fraction is exactly the strain component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) in the axes of the cube.

Lemma 3.16 Strain in pure shear (deformacija pri čistem strigu)

Let the material at the point \(P\) satisfy assumptions 1 to 5 of section 3.2.1: elasticity, linearity, isotropy (the rule that gives the strain components from the stress components is the same in every rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, with the same \(E\) and \(\nu\)), small strains and constant temperature. Here \(E\) is Young's modulus of the material and \(\nu\) its Poisson's ratio. Let the only nonzero stress components at the point \(P\) (forces along the faces) in some rectangular Cartesian coordinate system be \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \tau_0\). Then the only nonzero strain components at \(P\) in this system are

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = \frac{(1 + \nu)\,\tau_0}{E} . \tag{3.21}\]
Proof

We write the stress in axes along the diagonals, where it is the sum of two uniaxial stresses, add the two strains and carry them back.

  1. Take new axes with the unit vectors \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = (1, 0, 1)/\sqrt2\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} = (0, 1, 0)\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = (-1, 0, 1)/\sqrt2\), that is, along the diagonals \(AC\) and \(BD\) and perpendicular to the picture. The rows of the rotation matrix \(\mat Q\) are these three vectors (definition 2.44).
  2. By theorem 2.53 on the transformation of stress components, in the new axes \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tau_0\) (tension) and \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\tau_0\) (compression), and all other components are zero, as we computed in section 2.9.
  3. This is the sum of two states: in the first the only nonzero component is \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tau_0\), in the second \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\tau_0\).
  4. Here we use isotropy (assumption 3). Lemma 3.12 on uniaxial stress holds in every rectangular Cartesian coordinate system with the same \(E\) and \(\nu\), so also in the new axes. The first state gives \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tau_0/E\), \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\nu\,\tau_0/E\) and no shear components (the first rhombus of figure 3.62). Without isotropy this step could not be made: in a material with fibres, such as wood, the direction of the diagonal has a different modulus than the direction of an axis, and the relation we are proving does not hold for it.
  5. For the second state we use the lemma with the axis \(\bar z\) in the place of the first axis, as in section 3.2.4, and with the stress \(-\tau_0\). It gives \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\tau_0/E\), \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \nu\,\tau_0/E\) and no shear components (the second rhombus).
  6. By linearity (assumption 2) we add:
    \[\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{(1 + \nu)\,\tau_0}{E} , \qquad \bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \frac{-\nu\,\tau_0 + \nu\,\tau_0}{E} = 0 , \qquad \bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\frac{(1 + \nu)\,\tau_0}{E} ,\]
    and there are no shear components in the new axes (the third rhombus). We may add only while the material stays linear elastic, for steel that is below the yield stress.
  7. By lemma 2.55, \(\bar{\ten\varepsilon} = \mat Q\,\ten\varepsilon\,\mat Q^\T\). We multiply by \(\mat Q^\T\) from the left and by \(\mat Q\) from the right, where \(\mat Q^\T\mat Q = \mat I\) (definition 2.46) and the matrix product is associative (lemma 1.100):
    \[\mat Q^\T\bar{\ten\varepsilon}\,\mat Q = \mat I\,\ten\varepsilon\,\mat I = \ten\varepsilon .\]
  8. By definition 1.99 the entry \((i, j)\) of the product is \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}}\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}}\). Only \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = g\) and \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -g\) are nonzero, \(g = (1 + \nu)\,\tau_0/E\), so two terms remain:
    \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = g\,(Q_{\mathrm{xi}}\,Q_{\mathrm{xj}} - Q_{\mathrm{zi}}\,Q_{\mathrm{zj}}) .\]
  9. The row \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat Q\) is \((1, 0, 1)/\sqrt2\), the row \(z\) is \((-1, 0, 1)/\sqrt2\). For \(i = j = x\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = g\,(\tfrac12 - \tfrac12) = 0\), for \(i = j = z\) likewise \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\), and for \(i = x\) and \(j = z\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = g\,\big(\tfrac12 - (-\tfrac12)\big) = g\). Where \(i\) or \(j\) equals \(y\), \(Q_{\mathrm{xy}} = Q_{\mathrm{zy}} = 0\), so \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are zero. Only \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = (1 + \nu)\,\tau_0/E\) remains. In the axes of the cube this is the rhombus of figure 3.63, whose diagonal \(AC\) is longer by the fraction \(g\) and whose diagonal \(BD\) is shorter by the fraction \(g\).

Source: SADD §4.3.2 (PDF p. 95), CM (6.3.40) (PDF p. 267). The sources read the result off the general law for an isotropic material. The route through a tension and a compression along the diagonals is not from the sources.

The lemma confirms the third rhombus of figure 3.62 and adds what happens to the right angle. We look at the front face of the cube, the axis \(x\) points to the right, the axis \(z\) up. The square \(ABCD\) becomes a rhombus, longer along \(AC\) and shorter along \(BD\) by the fraction \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\), and its right angle at the corner \(A\) gets smaller (figure 3.63). That \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) is exactly the strain of the diagonal \(AC\) we also see from (1.61): the fibre in the direction \((1, 0, 1)/\sqrt2\) has the strain \(\tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0 + 0 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\).

Shear stress and shear strain are thus proportional, just like stress and strain in the tension test. Their ratio has its own name. Books measure it with the engineering shear strain \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) of section 1.17.4, and so do we.

Definition 3.17 Shear modulus (strižni modul)

Let the only nonzero stress components in a small piece of a linear elastic isotropic material be \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \tau_0 \neq 0\) (pure shear), and let \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) be the engineering shear strain that this stress causes. The shear modulus (strižni modul) of the material is the number

\[G = \frac{\tau_0}{\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}}} .\]

Source: SADD §4.3.2 (PDF p. 95), CM (6.3.40) (PDF p. 267), BOWER §3.2.5 (PDF p. 101).

By lemma 3.16 on strain in pure shear, the change of the right angle is \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 2\,(1 + \nu)\,\tau_0/E\), so

\[G = \frac{E}{2\,(1 + \nu)} , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 2G\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} . \tag{3.22}\]

The ratio does not depend on \(\tau_0\), so any nonzero stress determines it. At \(\tau_0 = 0\) the quotient would be \(0/0\), which is why the definition requires \(\tau_0 \neq 0\). For steel \(G = 196\ \text{GPa}/\big(2\,(1 + 0{,}3)\big) = 75{,}38\) GPa, less than half of \(E\) (for \(0 \le \nu \le 0{,}5\), \(G\) lies between \(E/3\) and \(E/2\)). BOWER also notes that it is smaller than \(E\) (§3.2.6, PDF p. 102). With the engineering shear strain the relation has the form \(\tau = G\,\gamma\), the same as \(\sigma = E\,\varepsilon\) in the tension test (CM (6.3.40), PDF p. 267). With our component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\), which is half of \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}}\), it carries a factor \(2\): \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 2G\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\). SADD writes the same, with the shear modulus \(\mu\) (SADD, PDF p. 95). When reading the sources one must therefore check which shear strain they use. The shear modulus can be measured directly, for example by twisting a thin tube, in whose wall pure shear arises (SADD §4.3.2, PDF p. 95, chapter 16). For an isotropic material it need not be measured, since \(E\) and \(\nu\) determine it.

Let us test this on a steel cube with the edge \(h = 10\) mm in pure shear with \(\tau_0 = 50\) MPa, as in section 2.6.6. By the lemma on strain in pure shear,

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \frac{\tau_0}{2G} = \frac{50 \cdot 10^6\ \text{Pa}}{2 \cdot 75{,}38 \cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa}} = 3{,}316 \cdot 10^{-4} , \qquad \gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 6{,}633 \cdot 10^{-4} .\]

The diagonal \(AC\) gets longer by the fraction \(3{,}316 \cdot 10^{-4}\), so with its length \(10\sqrt2\ \text{mm} = 14{,}14\) mm by \(4{,}690\) µm, and the diagonal \(BD\) gets shorter by the same. Let the cube be glued to the table by its bottom face, like the sheared cube of section 1.6.2. The displacement field \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = \gamma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,z\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) has zero displacement on the bottom face, where \(z = 0\), and by (1.59) exactly these strains: \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \tfrac12\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial x) = \tfrac12\,(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} + 0)\), and all other components are zero. The top face moves by

\[s = \gamma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,h = 6{,}633 \cdot 10^{-4} \cdot 10\ \text{mm} = 6{,}633\ \text{µm} .\]

By (2.63) of section 2.9.6 the sine of the angle by which the right angle at the corner \(A\) decreases is approximately \(2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = 6{,}633 \cdot 10^{-4}\), which is an angle of \(0{,}038^\circ\) (computed with NumPy). The rhombus of figure 3.63 has its bottom edge \(AB\) raised by an angle of about \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\). The glued cube is the same rhombus turned clockwise by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = 3{,}316 \cdot 10^{-4}\) rad, which is \(0{,}019^\circ\), so that its bottom edge lies on the table. A rotation changes no length, so it does not change the strains either.

Now we can also answer a question that we did not ask in section 1.6.2: what forces are needed to push the top face of the steel cube by \(s = 10\) µm? There \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = s/h = 0{,}001\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0{,}0005\). By the definition of the shear modulus, such a strain is caused by pure shear with

\[\tau_0 = G\,\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 75{,}38 \cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa} \cdot 0{,}001 = 75{,}38\ \text{MPa} .\]

On each face with the area \(100\) mm² \(= 10^{-4}\) m² the force is therefore \(75{,}38 \cdot 10^6\ \text{Pa} \cdot 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2 = 7538\) N (figure 3.64). We push the top face to the right, the glue pulls the bottom face to the left, we pull the right face up and the left face down. We look at the cube from the front, the axis \(x\) points to the right, the axis \(z\) up, and the corners \(C\) and \(D\) move to \(C_1\) and \(D_1\). Without the forces on the side faces the forces on the top and bottom faces would turn the cube, as we saw for pure shear in section 2.6.6, and the field \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}001\,z\) would not hold near the free side faces. The field of chapter 1 is thus an idealization that requires these four forces. Does the steel stay elastic? In pure shear the principal stresses are \(\tau_0\), \(0\) and \(-\tau_0\), so the largest shear stress over all faces is \(\tau_0\) (theorem 2.93). In the tension test steel starts to yield at \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa, when the largest shear stress on oblique cuts is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}/2 = 110\) MPa (lemma 2.19 on the largest shear stress in a bar). By the rule of section 2.4, that the largest shear stress roughly decides when metals start to yield, \(75{,}38\) MPa is below the limit, and the cube stays elastic.

3.2.7 The shear test

We measured the modulus of elasticity \(E\) in the tension test: the force is divided by the area, the elongation by the length, and the slope of the straight line is \(E\) (section 3.1.2). Can the shear modulus \(G\) be measured as directly, without \(E\) and \(\nu\)? It can. The test is the sheared cube of figure 3.64, only now we measure the force and the shift. It is called the shear test (strižni preizkus), because the material is loaded in shear, that is, by a force along a face and not perpendicular to it.

Let us put it together (figure 3.65). On the table we lay a stiff plate and fix it. On it we glue a block of the material we are measuring, with the length \(l\), the height \(h\) and the width \(b\), which points into the picture. We draw it grey and dashed, as it is before loading. We look at it from the front, the axis \(x\) points to the right, the axis \(z\) up. On the top face of the block we glue a second stiff plate. On the right the block is drawn once more from above, with the axis \(x\) to the right and the axis \(y\) up: its top face is a rectangle with the area \(A = l\,b\) with the sides \(l\) and \(b\). Now we pull the top plate to the right with the force \(F\), which we measure with a load cell, as in the tension test. The plate runs under a guide with rollers, which does not let it lift or tilt. The top plate moves to the right by \(\Delta x\), which we measure. The block leans into the orange parallelogram: the bottom face stays in place, the top face moves with the plate, and the left edge leans by the angle \(\gamma\).

From the measured force \(F\) and displacement \(\Delta x\) we compute the shear stress and the shear strain, just as in the tension test we computed \(\sigma\) and \(\varepsilon\) from the force and the elongation.

  1. The shear stress. The top plate is at rest, so the sum of the forces on it is zero (definition 2.3). In the direction of the axis \(x\) only our force \(F\) acts on it and the force with which the block pulls it back through the glue. This force therefore equals \(F\) in size. It is spread over the top face of the block with the area \(A\), so per unit area it is
    \[\tau = \frac{F}{A} = \frac{F}{l\,b} . \tag{3.23}\]
    This is the average of the stress component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) over the top face of the block. The force acts along the face, not perpendicular to it, so this is a shear stress. On the bottom face it is equally large and opposite, since the table holds the bottom plate with the force \(F\) to the left.
  2. The shear strain. Let us assume that the horizontal layers of the block slide along each other like the cards of the deck in figure 1.12, each in proportion to its height \(z\) above the bottom face: \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = (\Delta x/h)\,z\) and \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). On the bottom face the displacement is zero, on the top face \(\Delta x\). By (1.59) the only nonzero strain component is then \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \tfrac12\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial x) = \tfrac12\,\Delta x/h\), and the engineering shear strain is
    \[\gamma = 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \frac{\Delta x}{h} . \tag{3.24}\]
    This is the shift of the top face divided by the height of the block, just as \(\varepsilon = \Delta L/L\) is the elongation divided by the length. In the figure \(\Delta x/h\) is the tangent of the angle by which the left edge leans. For a small lean the tangent is almost equal to the angle in radians, so the figure simply labels this angle \(\gamma\). How close the two are, the last of the assumptions below tells.
  3. The shear modulus. By definition 3.17, it is the quotient of the stress \(\tau\) and the strain \(\gamma\),
    \[G = \frac{\tau}{\gamma} = \frac{F/A}{\Delta x/h} = \frac{F\,h}{A\,\Delta x} . \tag{3.25}\]

The two tests stand side by side like this.

tension test shear test
we measure the force \(F\) and the elongation \(\Delta L\) the force \(F\) and the shift \(\Delta x\)
the force acts perpendicular to the cross section with the area \(A\) along the face with the area \(A\)
stress \(\sigma = F/A\) \(\tau = F/A\)
strain \(\varepsilon = \Delta L/L\) \(\gamma = \Delta x/h\)
slope of the line \(E = \sigma/\varepsilon\) \(G = \tau/\gamma\)

Let us try it with numbers. Let a block of rubber have the length \(l = 100\) mm, the width \(b = 50\) mm and the height \(h = 10\) mm. Say that at the force \(F = 100\) N we measure the shift \(\Delta x = 0{,}04\) mm. Then

\[\begin{aligned} A &= 0{,}1\ \text{m} \cdot 0{,}05\ \text{m} = 0{,}005\ \text{m}^2 , & \tau &= \frac{100\ \text{N}}{0{,}005\ \text{m}^2} = 20\,000\ \text{Pa} , \\ \gamma &= \frac{0{,}04\ \text{mm}}{10\ \text{mm}} = 0{,}004 , & G &= \frac{20\,000\ \text{Pa}}{0{,}004} = 5 \cdot 10^6\ \text{Pa} = 5\ \text{MPa} . \end{aligned}\]

Is this a sensible number? Let us draw it on a logarithmic axis of the shear modulus, where each step between the marks means a ten times larger value, as in figure 1.22. For natural rubber BOWER gives \(E\) from \(0{,}01\) to \(0{,}1\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}49\) (BOWER, table 3.1, PDF p. 100). By (3.22), \(G = E/\big(2\,(1 + 0{,}49)\big)\) therefore lies between \(3{,}356\) and \(33{,}56\) MPa, which is the orange band, and our \(5\) MPa is in it. Steel with \(75{,}38\) GPa lies four decades further right, its shear modulus is \(15\,076\) times larger. The shift \(\Delta x = \tau\,h/G\) is inversely proportional to \(G\) at the same stress and height, so a steel block of the same size would at the same force shift that much less, by \(\Delta x = 20\,000\ \text{Pa} \cdot 10\ \text{mm}/(75{,}38 \cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa}) = 2{,}653 \cdot 10^{-6}\) mm. That is \(2{,}653\) nm instead of \(0{,}04\) mm for rubber, too little for such a gauge. For metals shear is therefore rather produced by twisting a thin tube (SADD §4.3.2, PDF p. 95, chapter 16).

What did we assume on the way? Three things, each with its reason, its limit and its cost.

  • The layers slide evenly. Why we may assume it: the plates are stiff and glued on, so the top face of the block moves as a whole while the bottom face stays in place, and the material is the same everywhere. Where it fails: at the left and the right side face of the block. No force acts on them, so the stress component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\) is zero there, and since the stress is symmetric, so is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\). Pure shear, however, needs forces on all four faces, also on the side faces. Near the ends of the block the state is therefore not pure shear. What this does to the result: \(\tau = F/A\) stays the exact average, since it follows from the equilibrium of the plate alone, but in the middle of the block the shear stress is somewhat larger than the average, because the ends carry less. The measured \(G\) is therefore somewhat too small. By Saint-Venant's principle the disturbance reaches only near the ends (section 2.2), but how far, the principle does not say. That is why the block is long and low, here \(l = 10\,h\). To get a feeling for the size, let us draw below the block the shear stress along its length. The average \(20\) kPa is a horizontal line over the whole length. Suppose that a piece of the length \(h\) at each end carried no shear at all. Then the stress in the middle would be \(F/\big((l - 2h)\,b\big) = 25\) kPa instead of \(20\) kPa. The area under each line, stress times length, is the force per unit width of the block, \(F/b = 2\) N/mm, and it is the same in both cases. So the area the ends lose, \(2 \cdot 20\ \text{kPa} \cdot 10\ \text{mm} = 400\) kPa mm, equals the area the middle gains, \(5\ \text{kPa} \cdot 80\ \text{mm} = 400\) kPa mm. The top plate moves with the middle of the block, which is sheared by \(25\) kPa, while we compute \(G\) with \(20\) kPa. We would measure it by the factor \(20/25 = 0{,}8\), that is a fifth too small. This is an estimate under that supposition, not a calculation, and the supposition is too crude. Let us also compute the true distribution. We divide the block into small rectangles, \(140\) along the length and \(14\) along the height, and in each we require equilibrium and Hooke's law (the finite element method, chapter 15). We take rubber with \(\nu = 0{,}49\) and a block that is very wide in the direction \(y\). We read the stress at half the height and draw it along the axis \(x\) from the free face on. At the free side face it is indeed zero, but it reaches the average \(20\) kPa already at about \(0{,}4\,h\). Since the same force \(F\) goes across this whole plane, what the end does not carry is made up elsewhere: a little further on the stress exceeds the average, up to \(22{,}1\) kPa, and from about \(1{,}5\,h\) on it is constant, \(20{,}46\) kPa, not \(25\) kPa as in the estimate, in which a piece of the length \(h\) carries nothing. The measured \(G\) is therefore \(20/20{,}46 = 0{,}978\) of the true one, that is too small by only \(2{,}2\) %, not by a fifth. For a very narrow block the error is \(3{,}0\) %, for ours with \(b = 5\,h\) we expect a value in between. The error is proportional to \(h/l\): at \(l = 5\,h\) it is \(4{,}5\) %, at \(l = 20\,h\) only \(1{,}1\) %.
  • The plates stay parallel. The force \(F\) on the top plate and the force \(F\) on the bottom plate are equal and opposite, but they do not lie on one line. Let us draw the plates and the block as one body with both forces \(F\), which are about the height \(h\) apart. Together they try to turn the body clockwise, with the moment \(F\,h = 100\ \text{N} \cdot 0{,}01\ \text{m} = 1\) N m (definition 2.37). In pure shear this moment is balanced by the forces on the side faces. Here the side faces are free, so it must be balanced by the guide and the table.
