The guide presses the top plate down nearer the left end, where the body would rise, the table pushes the bottom plate up nearer the right end, where the body would sink, and these two forces \(R\) turn it the other way. They are at most about the length \(l\) apart, so each is at least \(F\,h/l = 100\ \text{N} \cdot 10\ \text{mm}/100\ \text{mm} = 10\) N, a tenth of the force \(F\). For a cube with \(l = h\) they would be at least as large as \(F\) itself. This is the second reason for a long and low block. Without the guide the top plate would tilt, and \(\Delta x\) would no longer measure shear alone.
  • The strain is small and the material linear elastic. Equation (1.59) may be used only for small strains (chapter 1). Here \(\Delta x/h = 0{,}004\), the angle \(\gamma\) measures \(0{,}2292^\circ\), and its tangent differs from the angle in radians by five millionths of its value. At \(\Delta x/h = 0{,}1\) the difference is \(0{,}33\) %. Rubber can take much larger tilts, but there the relation between \(\tau\) and \(\gamma\) is no longer a straight line, and \(G\) of (3.25) is only its initial slope. For rubber at large strains books use different laws (BOWER §3.5, PDF p. 120).

In the lectures the axes are numbered \(1\), \(2\), \(3\), so there the shear stress is \(\sigma_{12} = F/A\), the engineering shear strain \(\gamma_{12} = \Delta x/h\) and \(G = \sigma_{12}/\gamma_{12} = \sigma_{12}/(2\,\varepsilon_{12})\). The shear modulus there also has the symbol \(\mu\), as in SADD. One more difference of notation concerns the tension test: the lectures divide the lateral strain by the diameter after loading, \((d - d_0)/d\), while the book in definition 3.8 divides by the diameter before loading, \((d - d_0)/d_0\). For the steel bar of section 3.1.8, which gets thinner from \(d_0 = 10\) mm by \(1{,}949 \cdot 10^{-3}\) mm, the two differ by the fraction \(1{,}949 \cdot 10^{-4}\), that is, by \(0{,}02\) %, and Poisson's ratio would be \(0{,}30006\) instead of \(0{,}3\). For small strains it makes no difference, for large ones it does.

3.2.8 Any two constants determine the others

For an isotropic material we now have four numbers, each from its own test: \(E\) and \(\nu\) from tension in one direction, \(K\) from pressure from all sides and \(G\) from shear. Only two of them are independent, since we computed \(K\) and \(G\) from \(E\) and \(\nu\) (equations (3.20) and (3.22)). May we also choose differently, for instance measure \(K\) and \(G\) and compute \(E\) and \(\nu\) from them? We may. Let us turn the two equations around, in small steps.

  1. We multiply both equations by the denominator, so that the fractions disappear:
    \[3K\,(1 - 2\nu) = E , \qquad 2G\,(1 + \nu) = E .\]
  2. The right sides are equal, so the left sides are equal too. We multiply out the brackets:
    \[3K - 6K\,\nu = 2G + 2G\,\nu .\]
  3. We move the terms with \(\nu\) to the right and the term \(2G\) to the left, and take \(\nu\) out of the brackets:
    \[3K - 2G = (6K + 2G)\,\nu = 2\,(3K + G)\,\nu .\]
  4. We divide by \(2\,(3K + G)\), which we may, because \(K\) and \(G\) are positive:
    \[\nu = \frac{3K - 2G}{2\,(3K + G)} .\]
  5. We compute \(1 + \nu\) by writing the one with the same denominator:
    \[1 + \nu = \frac{2\,(3K + G) + 3K - 2G}{2\,(3K + G)} = \frac{9K}{2\,(3K + G)} .\]
  6. We put this into the second equation of step 1:
    \[E = 2G\,(1 + \nu) = \frac{9KG}{3K + G} .\]

Steel, \(K = 163{,}3\) GPa, \(G = 75{,}38\) GPa:

\[\nu = \frac{3 \cdot 163{,}3 - 2 \cdot 75{,}38}{2\,(3 \cdot 163{,}3 + 75{,}38)} = \frac{339{,}14}{1130{,}56} = 0{,}3000 , \qquad E = \frac{9 \cdot 163{,}3 \cdot 75{,}38}{3 \cdot 163{,}3 + 75{,}38}\ \text{GPa} = \frac{110\,786}{565{,}28}\ \text{GPa} = 196{,}0\ \text{GPa} ,\]

which are the two numbers we started from. It works the same way with any other pair. The table collects three pairs (SADD, table 4.1, PDF p. 97, checked with SymPy).

known numbers \(E\) \(\nu\) \(K\) \(G\)
\(E\), \(\nu\) \(E\) \(\nu\) \(\dfrac{E}{3\,(1 - 2\nu)}\) \(\dfrac{E}{2\,(1 + \nu)}\)
\(E\), \(G\) \(E\) \(\dfrac{E}{2G} - 1\) \(\dfrac{E\,G}{3\,(3G - E)}\) \(G\)
\(K\), \(G\) \(\dfrac{9KG}{3K + G}\) \(\dfrac{3K - 2G}{2\,(3K + G)}\) \(K\) \(G\)

An isotropic linear elastic material is thus described by any two of the numbers \(E\), \(\nu\), \(K\), \(G\), which tension, pressure from all sides and shear give, and the third and the fourth follow (SADD, PDF p. 96). Which pair we take is a matter of convenience: \(E\) and \(\nu\) are the easiest to measure, while \(K\) and \(G\) separate the change of volume from the change of shape, which we will use in section 3.2.11. The table holds only for an isotropic material. In a material with fibres, such as wood, the shear modulus does not follow from \(E\) and \(\nu\) and has to be measured separately (section 3.4).

3.2.9 The law for all components

Now we know the response to all simple stress states. Every state is the sum of three uniaxial stresses along the axes and three pure shears, one in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\), one in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(z\) and one in the plane of the axes \(y\) and \(z\), and by linearity we add their strains.

Let us draw these states on a small cube (figure 3.69), which we view each time along one axis, the axes next to a panel tell along which. The cube before loading we draw grey dashed. In the first panel the normal stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) pull it along the axes, and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) toward us, which we draw as a small circle with a dot. The cube stretches into a box, its angles stay right. In the second panel the shear stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) acts along four faces and skews the cube into a rhombus: the angle at the corner is smaller than a right angle, while the lengths of the edges do not change at small strains: the end of an edge of length 1 moves across the edge by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), so by Pythagoras' theorem the edge is \(\sqrt{1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}^2}\) long, at \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0{,}001\) only \(5 \cdot 10^{-7}\) longer. The third and the fourth panel are the same shear in the other two planes, with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\). Under each panel we write the strains its state causes, and the plus signs say that we add the states.

Often we also need the reverse rule, which gives the stresses from the strains, for example when we know the displacement field and look for the stresses.

From history

Navier, Poisson and Cauchy built the theory on molecules with forces along the lines joining them (figure 1.7), as we saw in section 3.1.8. For a general substance, in which each of the six stress components is a linear function of the six strain components, Poisson and Cauchy assumed \(6 \cdot 6 = 36\) constants. The molecular assumption reduced them to 15, and for a substance that is the same in all directions to one (TIMO, PDF p. 189). From this theory Poisson also derived that the shear modulus is \(0{,}4\,E\) and the bulk modulus \(\tfrac23 E\) (TIMO, PDF p. 189, LOVE, PDF p. 29). Indeed, at \(\nu = 1/4\) equations (3.22) and (3.20) give \(G = E/(2 \cdot 1{,}25) = 0{,}4\,E\) and \(K = E/(3 \cdot 0{,}5) = \tfrac23 E\). The ratio \(K/G\) is therefore \(5:3\) for every such substance.

Two constants were also obtained by George Green, who did not want to assume molecules but started from the principle of conservation of energy (TIMO, PDF p. 190-191, section 3.6.5). George Gabriel Stokes noticed that resistance to compression and resistance to shearing are the two fundamental resistances of a substance that is the same in all directions, and introduced both moduli (LOVE, PDF p. 29). He would not accept Poisson's conclusion that the ratio of the two is always \(5:3\), because liquids, soft solids and hard solids resist compression and change of shape in very different ratios (LOVE, PDF p. 29). We test Stokes' objection on the table in section 3.1.8. On the horizontal axis we put Poisson's ratio \(\nu\), on the vertical one the ratio \(K/G\) on a logarithmic scale. From (3.22) and (3.20) it follows that \(K/G = 2\,(1 + \nu)/\big(3\,(1 - 2\nu)\big)\), which is \(5:3\) only at \(\nu = 1/4\), for example for nylon. For mild steel with \(\nu = 0{,}30\) we get \(K/G = 2{,}17\). For natural rubber with \(\nu = 0{,}49\) we have \(K = 16{,}7\,E\) and \(G = 0{,}34\,E\), so \(K/G = 49{,}7\): rubber is hard to compress but changes its shape easily in shear (BOWER, Table 3.1, PDF p. 100).

Gabriel Lamé in a book of 1852 accepted, because of the results of experiments, that a substance which is the same in all directions is described by two constants (LOVE, PDF p. 30, TIMO, PDF p. 125). In a book of 1859 he gave up Navier's derivation with molecular forces, used only the statics of a rigid body as Cauchy did, and assumed that the stresses are linear functions of the strains. So he needs no hypothesis about molecules, and the two constants are obtained from a simple tension test and from a test in which we twist a bar (TIMO, PDF p. 126). This is exactly what we have done: we built the law without molecules, from the tension test and the pure shear.

Let us return to the reverse rule, which gives the stresses from the strains. Two combinations of the numbers \(E\) and \(\nu\) appear in the reverse rule, which books name after Lamé (CM, PDF p. 266, SADD names only the first after him and the second the shear modulus, PDF p. 93).

Definition 3.18 Lamé constants (Laméjevi konstanti)

The Lamé constants (Laméjevi konstanti) of a linear elastic isotropic material with Young's modulus \(E\) and Poisson's ratio \(\nu\), where \(\nu \neq -1\) and \(\nu \neq \tfrac12\), are the numbers

\[\lambda = \frac{\nu\,E}{(1 + \nu)(1 - 2\nu)} , \qquad \mu = \frac{E}{2\,(1 + \nu)} . \tag{3.26}\]

Source: CM (6.3.33) (PDF p. 266), SADD (4.2.7) (PDF p. 93) and Table 4.1 (PDF p. 97), BOWER §3.2.5 (PDF p. 101).

The constant \(\mu\) has the same formula as the shear modulus in (3.22), so \(\mu = G\). For steel \(\lambda = 196\ \text{GPa} \cdot 0{,}3/\big((1 + 0{,}3)(1 - 2 \cdot 0{,}3)\big) = 113{,}1\) GPa and \(\mu = 75{,}38\) GPa. The letter \(\lambda\) is the established one for this constant in books (CM (6.3.32), SADD (4.2.7)), although in section 2.11 we used it for an eigenvalue, and in section 2.13 for a ratio of lengths. Where the meanings meet, we will say which one is meant.

Below, \(\tr\ten\varepsilon = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) denotes the trace of the matrix of the small strain tensor, the sum of its diagonal entries (section 1.17.4), and \(\tr\ten\sigma = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) the trace of the stress matrix. The trace of the strain matrix is the volumetric strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\).

Theorem 3.19 Hooke's law for an isotropic material (Hookov zakon za izotropen material)

Let the material at every point of the body satisfy assumptions 1 to 5 of section 3.2.1: elasticity, linearity, isotropy (the rule that gives the strain components from the stress components is the same in every rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, with the same \(E\) and \(\nu\)), small strains and constant temperature. Here \(E\) is Young's modulus of the material and \(\nu\) its Poisson's ratio. Then at every point of the body and in every rectangular Cartesian coordinate system:

1. Strains from stresses.

\[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} &= \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \nu\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}})}{E} , \qquad & \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \frac{1 + \nu}{E}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} &= \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} - \nu\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}})}{E} , \qquad & \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} &= \frac{1 + \nu}{E}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} &= \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} - \nu\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}})}{E} , \qquad & \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} &= \frac{1 + \nu}{E}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} . \end{aligned} \tag{3.27}\]
\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \frac{1 + \nu}{E}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} - \frac{\nu}{E}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{kk}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} , \qquad i, j = x, y, z . \tag{3.27}\]

2. Stresses from strains. If \(\nu \neq -1\) and \(\nu \neq \tfrac12\), then

\[\ten\sigma = \lambda\,(\tr\ten\varepsilon)\,\mat I + 2\mu\,\ten\varepsilon , \tag{3.28}\]
\[\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kk}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} + 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} , \qquad i, j = x, y, z , \tag{3.28}\]

where \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) are the Lamé constants of the material and \(\mat I\) is the identity matrix, in components

\[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} &= \lambda\,\tr\ten\varepsilon + 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} , \qquad & \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} &= 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} &= \lambda\,\tr\ten\varepsilon + 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} , \qquad & \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} &= 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} &= \lambda\,\tr\ten\varepsilon + 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} , \qquad & \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} &= 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} . \end{aligned}\]
Proof

1. Strains from stresses. We split the stress into six simple states and add their strains by linearity.

  1. By theorem 2.41 on the symmetry of stress, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\). We therefore write the stress matrix as the sum of four matrices, added entry by entry:
    \[\ten\sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} & 0 \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} \\ 0 & \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} & 0 \end{bmatrix} .\]
    In figure 3.69 these are the four panels from left to right: the first matrix, the second, the third and the fourth.
  2. The first matrix is three normal stresses without shear. By (3.19) it causes the normal strains of the left column of (3.27) and no shear strains, the angles of the cube stay right.
  3. The third matrix is pure shear with \(\tau_0 = \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\). By lemma 3.16 on strain in pure shear it causes only \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = (1 + \nu)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}/E\).
  4. The lemma on strain in pure shear holds in every rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, because by assumption 3 the material is isotropic. If we rename the axis \(y\) to \(x\), the axis \(z\) to \(y\) and the axis \(x\) to \(z\), the second matrix becomes pure shear between the first and the third axis, so it causes only \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} = (1 + \nu)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}/E\). The figure says the same: the second panel is the third with two other letters at the axes.
  5. If we rename the axis \(z\) to \(x\), the axis \(x\) to \(y\) and the axis \(y\) to \(z\), the fourth matrix becomes pure shear between the first and the third axis, so it causes only \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zy}} = (1 + \nu)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}/E\).
  6. By linearity (assumption 2 of section 3.2.1) the strains are the sums of the strains of steps 2 to 5. This is where the assumption enters, and without it the step is not allowed: in a material whose stress is not proportional to the strain, the response to a sum of stresses is not the sum of the responses. For steel it holds up to the yield stress, up to strains of about \(0{,}00112\) (section 2.2). Each component receives a contribution from one step only, and we get (3.27).

2. Stresses from strains. We solve the equations of item 1 for the stresses, first for the sum of the normal stresses.

  1. We add the three equations of the left column of (3.27). Each normal stress appears once with the factor \(1\) and twice with the factor \(-\nu\), so \(\tr\ten\varepsilon = (1 - 2\nu)\,\tr\ten\sigma/E\).
  2. Since \(\nu \neq \tfrac12\), we may divide by \(1 - 2\nu\): \(\tr\ten\sigma = E\,\tr\ten\varepsilon/(1 - 2\nu)\).
  3. In the first equation of the left column we write \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \tr\ten\sigma - \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and multiply by \(E\): \(E\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \nu\,(\tr\ten\sigma - \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}) = (1 + \nu)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \nu\,\tr\ten\sigma\).
  4. Since \(\nu \neq -1\), we may divide by \(1 + \nu\), and we put in step 2:
    \[\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{E}{1 + \nu}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \frac{\nu}{1 + \nu}\,\tr\ten\sigma = \frac{E}{1 + \nu}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \frac{\nu\,E}{(1 + \nu)(1 - 2\nu)}\,\tr\ten\varepsilon = 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \lambda\,\tr\ten\varepsilon ,\]
    where we used (3.26), from which \(E/(1 + \nu) = 2\mu\).
  5. In the same way the second and third equations of the left column give \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\).
  6. From the right column, multiplied by \(E/(1 + \nu) = 2\mu\), follow \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\).
  7. The diagonal of the matrix \(\lambda\,(\tr\ten\varepsilon)\,\mat I + 2\mu\,\ten\varepsilon\) is \(\lambda\,\tr\ten\varepsilon + 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and likewise, off the diagonal stands \(2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), since \(\mat I\) has ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere (definition 1.108). By steps 4 to 6 it equals \(\ten\sigma\), which is (3.28).

Source: SADD (4.2.7), (4.2.8), (4.2.10), (4.2.11) (PDF pp. 93-94), CM (6.3.32)-(6.3.35) (PDF pp. 266-267), BOWER §3.2.2 (PDF pp. 97-98). SADD and CM write the law with indices, CM with the trace as we do. SADD derives it from the condition that the material constants do not change when the axes turn, and then explains the meaning of the constants from it with tension, shear and pressure (SADD §4.3, PDF pp. 94-96). We went the other way.

The law is named after Hooke, whom we met in section 1.1 and who wrote in 1678 that the deformation of an elastic body is proportional to the force (SADD, PDF p. 93). What does item 1 say? The normal strains depend only on the normal stresses (the first panel of figure 3.69), and each shear strain only on the shear stress with the same two indices (the other three). A shear stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) therefore changes no length along the axes, and a normal stress no right angle between the axes. A material with all these properties is described by only two numbers, \(E\) and \(\nu\). All the others, \(G\), \(K\), \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\), we compute from them (SADD, Table 4.1, PDF p. 97).

Let us test the law on a small piece of a thin steel plate in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\), which in figure 3.71 we view from above on the left and from the side on the right. We pull the plate with the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 100\) MPa in the direction of the axis \(x\) and with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 50\) MPa in the direction of the axis \(y\), and at the same time shear it with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 30\) MPa. The two faces of the plate are free, so by Cauchy's formula \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) on them. The plate is thin, so we assume that these components are zero inside it too. Such a state is called plane stress (ravninsko napetostno stanje) (BOWER §3.2.3, PDF p. 99).

What does this assumption do to the result? Take the opposite extreme (figure 3.72), a piece whose surroundings do not let its thickness change, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\). We view both pieces from the side and pull them with the same \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) as before. The third equation of the left column of (3.27) then demands \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \nu\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}) = 0{,}3 \cdot 150 = 45\) MPa: the surroundings must pull both faces outward, otherwise the piece would get thinner as on the left, where the faces are free. The first equation gives \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = (100 - 0{,}3 \cdot (50 + 45))/196\,000 = 3{,}648 \cdot 10^{-4}\), which is 16 % less than with the free faces below. The difference is \(\nu\,\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}/E = 0{,}3 \cdot 45/196\,000 = 0{,}689 \cdot 10^{-4}\): the pull \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) shortens the piece in the direction of the axis \(x\), as tension makes a bar narrower (section 3.1.8). So the assumption is right for a thin plate loaded only in its own plane, and wrong where something presses on a face or where the piece is thick.

By item 1, with all stresses in MPa and \(E = 196\,000\) MPa,

\[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} &= \frac{100 - 0{,}3 \cdot 50}{196\,000} = 4{,}3367 \cdot 10^{-4} , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} &= \frac{50 - 0{,}3 \cdot 100}{196\,000} = 1{,}0204 \cdot 10^{-4} , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} &= \frac{0 - 0{,}3 \cdot (100 + 50)}{196\,000} = -2{,}2959 \cdot 10^{-4} , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \frac{(1 + 0{,}3) \cdot 30}{196\,000} = 1{,}9898 \cdot 10^{-4} , \end{aligned}\]

and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\). Figure 3.71 shows these strains. The piece gets longer in the direction of the axis \(x\), and \(4{,}25\) times less in the direction of the axis \(y\). It is drawn without rotation, so each of the two edges tilts by the angle \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), the right angle between them gets smaller by \(2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 3{,}98 \cdot 10^{-4}\), and the square becomes a parallelogram. The plate gets thinner, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} < 0\), although \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\): the tensions along the axes \(x\) and \(y\) thin it, as tension thins a bar (section 3.1.8).

Now we go back with item 2, with \(\lambda = 113\,080\) MPa and \(2\mu = 150\,770\) MPa, and build each component of the stress from two bars (figure 3.73), each in its own row. The trace is \(\tr\ten\varepsilon = (4{,}3367 + 1{,}0204 - 2{,}2959) \cdot 10^{-4} = 3{,}0612 \cdot 10^{-4}\), so \(\lambda\,\tr\ten\varepsilon = 34{,}62\) MPa, the same in all three normal stresses, since \(\mat I\) has ones only on the diagonal. When we add the term \(2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) to it, for \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) \(2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and for \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) \(2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), we get the sums

\[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} &= 34{,}62 + 150\,770 \cdot 4{,}3367 \cdot 10^{-4} = 34{,}62 + 65{,}38 = 100\ \text{MPa} , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} &= 34{,}62 - 150\,770 \cdot 2{,}2959 \cdot 10^{-4} = 34{,}62 - 34{,}62 = 0 . \end{aligned}\]

In the same way we get \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 50\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 150\,770 \cdot 1{,}9898 \cdot 10^{-4} = 30\) MPa, in which the first term is absent, because \(\mat I\) has zeros off the diagonal (checked with NumPy). For \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) the term \(\lambda\,\tr\ten\varepsilon\), which belongs to the change of volume, and the term \(2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), which belongs to the thinning, cancel exactly: the orange bar goes from the end of the blue one back to zero.

Books write the law in different ways. SADD writes the normal stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{x}}\), the shear stresses \(\tau_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and the strains \(e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(e_{\mathrm{xy}}\), with the same meaning as our \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) (SADD (4.2.8), (4.2.11), PDF pp. 93-94). CM writes item 2 as \(\ten\sigma = 2\mu\,\ten\varepsilon + \lambda\,\tr(\ten\varepsilon)\,\mat I\) (CM (6.3.32), PDF p. 266). BOWER (PDF pp. 97-98) and CM ((6.3.39), PDF p. 267) also write the law with a \(6 \times 6\) matrix, in which \(2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) stands in place of \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), and BOWER warns about it explicitly. We will meet this form in section 3.4. In the lectures the axes are numbered, \(\varepsilon_{11}\) is our \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), and item 1 has \(1/(2\mu)\) in place of \((1 + \nu)/E\), which by (3.26) is the same number.

3.2.10 The hanging bar

Let us return to the steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m with a diameter of 10 mm that hangs under its own weight. It is held in the idealized way of section 1.7.1: only the point \(O\), the centre of the top face, is fixed, and an upward force distributed evenly over the whole top face acts on that face. The axis \(x\) points from \(O\) vertically down, the axes \(y\) and \(z\) lie horizontally. In chapter 1 we took the displacement field from the books,

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, z) &= a\,(2Lx - x^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2) , \\ u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z) &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y , \\ u_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, z) &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,z , \end{aligned}\]

with \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\) m⁻¹ ((1.19)). Does this field agree with Hooke's law?

We know the stress from chapter 2. At the depth \(x\) the normal stress on the cross section is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \rho g\,(L - x)\) ((2.5)), and all other stress components are zero, because each cross section carries the part of the bar below it evenly, and neighbouring parts of the bar pass only vertical forces to each other (CM Example 7.3.2, equation (2), PDF p. 305). At every point of the bar there is thus uniaxial stress (figure 3.74). Take a thin piece of the bar at the depth \(x\), enlarged in the middle of the figure. The part of the bar above it pulls its top face up with the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(x)\), the part below it pulls the bottom face down with the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(x + \Delta x)\), and the thickness of the piece is \(\Delta x\). By Hooke's law, item 1, the strains are

\[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} &= \frac{\rho g\,(L - x)}{E} = 2a\,(L - x) , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} &= -\nu\,\frac{\rho g\,(L - x)}{E} = -\nu \cdot 2a\,(L - x) , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} &= 0 , \end{aligned}\]

where we used \(a = \rho g/(2E)\) from section 3.1. Before loading the piece is \(\Delta y\) wide and \(\Delta x\) high, its outline is grey dashed. After loading it is \((1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}})\,\Delta x\) high and \((1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}})\,\Delta y\) wide.

Now we compute the strains from the field by (1.59). We computed the partial derivatives in section 1.7.2.

  1. \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x = 2a\,(L - x)\), the slice gets longer along the axis \(x\).
  2. \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\), the slice gets narrower.
  3. \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x) = \tfrac12\,(-0{,}6\,a\,y + 0{,}6\,a\,y) = 0\), and likewise \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \tfrac12\,(-0{,}6\,a\,z + 0{,}6\,a\,z) = 0\).
  4. \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = \tfrac12\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial z + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial y) = \tfrac12\,(0 + 0) = 0\). There are no shear strains, the angles of the slice stay right.

At every point of the bar the field gives exactly the strains that Hooke's law demands, if \(-\nu \cdot 2a = -0{,}6\,a\), that is, \(\nu = 0{,}3\) (checked with SymPy). The number \(0{,}3\) in the field is indeed Poisson's ratio of steel, as section 3.1 anticipated, and the field agrees with the stress and with Hooke's law at every point. At the depth \(x = 5\) m, for example at the point \(P\) of section 1.7.1,

\[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} &= 7800 \cdot 9{,}81 \cdot 5\ \text{Pa} = 0{,}3826\ \text{MPa} , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} &= \frac{0{,}3826 \cdot 10^6\ \text{Pa}}{196 \cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa}} = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} &= -0{,}3 \cdot 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} = -5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} . \end{aligned}\]

So a slice at this depth, \(\Delta x = 1\) mm thick, is pulled by the upper part of the bar with the stress \(0{,}3826\) MPa, it gets longer by \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\) mm, and its diameter of 10 mm gets smaller by \(5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-6}\) mm. We multiplied the strain at the depth of 5 m by the thickness of the slice. This is accurate enough because the stresses on the upper and the lower face of the slice are nearly equal: over 1 mm the stress, and with it the strain, decreases by only \(0{,}02\) %, so the true elongation is only \(0{,}01\) % smaller (checked with SymPy).

What does this test not show? For this to really be the field of the hanging bar, the stress must also satisfy the equilibrium equations, which we checked in section 2.7, and the conditions on the surface of the bar and where it is held. How to find such a field without taking it from books we will see in chapter 11.

3.2.11 Volume and shape

Under even pressure the cube only got smaller, in pure shear it only changed its shape. Can every strain be split into these two parts, and is each caused by its own part of the stress? As in section 2.12 we split the stress into the mean stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = \tfrac13\,\tr\ten\sigma\) and the deviator \(\ten s = \ten\sigma - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\,\mat I\) (definition 2.98). In the same section (definition 2.114) we split the strain in the same way into the spherical part \(\tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\mat I\), where \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = \tr\ten\varepsilon\) is the volumetric strain, and the deviatoric strain

\[\ten e = \ten\varepsilon - \tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\mat I .\]

The spherical part (figure) lengthens every edge of a cube by the same fraction, \(\tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\), in the figure \(0{,}1\), and changes only the size. The deviatoric strain (figure) lengthens the cube in some directions and shortens it in others, so that its three normal strains add up to zero, in the figure \(0{,}2\), \(0\) and \(-0{,}2\). Its trace is \(\tr\ten e = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} - \tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} \cdot 3 = 0\), so by lemma 2.77 on the change of volume it does not change the volume up to terms that are products of strains, it changes only the shape (for normal strains alone step 4 of section 3.2.5 already shows this). In the figure the right rectangle has the area \(1{,}2 \cdot 0{,}8 = 0{,}96\) of the area of the square, and since \(e_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\), its volume is also \(0{,}96\) of the original. Missing is \(0{,}04 = 0{,}2 \cdot 0{,}2\), the product of the strains \(0{,}2\) and \(-0{,}2\), which is large only because the strains in the figure are strongly exaggerated. When the entries of the matrix \(\ten e\) are at most \(0{,}001\) in absolute value, by point 2 of the lemma the volume changes by at most \(6 \cdot 0{,}001^2 + 6 \cdot 0{,}001^3 = 6{,}006 \cdot 10^{-6}\) of the original, which is less than \(1\) % of the strain \(0{,}001\) itself. How are the two parts related to the stress?

  1. By (3.28), the stress is \(\ten\sigma = \lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\mat I + 2\mu\,\ten\varepsilon\). The trace of a sum is the sum of the traces, and the trace of the identity matrix is \(3\), so \(\tr\ten\sigma = 3\lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} + 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\).
  2. The mean stress is a third of this, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = (\lambda + \tfrac23\,\mu)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\).
  3. We put in (3.26) and add the fractions over the common denominator \(3\,(1 + \nu)(1 - 2\nu)\):
    \[\lambda + \tfrac23\,\mu = \frac{3\nu\,E + (1 - 2\nu)\,E}{3\,(1 + \nu)(1 - 2\nu)} = \frac{(1 + \nu)\,E}{3\,(1 + \nu)(1 - 2\nu)} = \frac{E}{3\,(1 - 2\nu)} = K\]
    by (3.20). Therefore \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = K\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\): the mean stress decides only how much the cube grows.
  4. The stress deviator is \(\ten s = \ten\sigma - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\,\mat I\). We insert \(\ten\sigma\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\):
    \[\ten s = \lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\mat I + 2\mu\,\ten\varepsilon - (\lambda + \tfrac23\,\mu)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\mat I .\]
    We combine the terms with \(\mat I\):
    \[\ten s = 2\mu\,\ten\varepsilon - \tfrac23\,\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\mat I .\]
    We factor out \(2\mu\):
    \[\ten s = 2\mu\,(\ten\varepsilon - \tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\mat I) .\]
  5. The expression in brackets is \(\ten e\), and \(\mu = G\), so \(\ten s = 2G\,\ten e\): the stress deviator decides only how the cube changes its shape.

For \(\nu \neq -1\) and \(\nu \neq \tfrac12\), where (3.28) holds, Hooke's law thus splits into two independent parts,

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = K\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} , \qquad \ten s = 2G\,\ten e . \tag{3.29}\]

The mean stress changes only the volume, and the bulk modulus tells how strongly the material resists this. The stress deviator changes only the shape, and the shear modulus tells how strongly the material resists a change of shape (figure 3.75). The figure shows the same: the whole strain \(\ten\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0{,}3\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -0{,}1\) is equal to the spherical part \(\tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\mat I\) plus the deviatoric strain \(\ten e\), and the stress \(\ten\sigma = \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\,\mat I + \ten s\) splits in the same way. In pure shear \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = 0\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = 0\), everything is a change of shape. Under even pressure \(\ten e = 0\) and \(\ten s = 0\), everything is a change of volume.

Let us check the split with numbers too, on the plate of figure 3.71. The mean stress is a third of the sum of the three normal stresses, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = (100 + 50 + 0)/3 = 50\) MPa. The bulk modulus of steel is \(K = 196\,000/(3 \cdot 0{,}4) = 163\,333\) MPa, and the volumetric strain of the plate is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = 3{,}0612 \cdot 10^{-4}\), the sum of the three normal strains. Indeed \(K\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = 163\,333 \cdot 3{,}0612 \cdot 10^{-4} = 50{,}00\) MPa. The deviator has \(s_{\mathrm{xx}} = 100 - 50 = 50\) MPa, the deviatoric strain \(e_{\mathrm{xx}} = (4{,}3367 - \tfrac13 \cdot 3{,}0612) \cdot 10^{-4} = 3{,}3163 \cdot 10^{-4}\), and \(2G\,e_{\mathrm{xx}} = 150\,770 \cdot 3{,}3163 \cdot 10^{-4} = 50{,}00\) MPa. The shear is all in the deviator, \(s_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 30\) MPa and \(e_{\mathrm{xy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\). So half of the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) enlarges the volume of the plate, and the other half changes its shape (checked with NumPy).

None of our sources writes the split in this form in a section of its own. We assembled it from the split of the strain (SADD (2.5.1), (2.5.2), PDF p. 49), the split of the stress (SADD (3.5.1), (3.5.2), PDF p. 72) and the bulk modulus (SADD (4.3.1), PDF p. 96).

One more property follows from the law, which isotropic materials have and others need not have. Every principal direction of stress is also a principal direction of strain (section 2.11). What this means is shown in figure 3.76, where we look at the same stress at the same point on two small squares cut in different directions and drawn grey dashed before loading, the axes are the same for both. The left one we cut along the principal directions of stress. On the face with the normal \(\vek n\) acts the force per unit area \(\sigma_1\,\vek n\), perpendicular to the face, and on the neighbouring face again only a perpendicular force. In the axes along the edges of this square the stress therefore has only normal components, and by item 1 of Hooke's law, which holds in every rectangular coordinate system, there is no shear strain. The square becomes a rectangle, its angles stay right, and the fibre along \(\vek n\) gets longer without turning. This is exactly what it means that \(\vek n\) is a principal direction of strain. The right one we cut along the axes \(x\) and \(z\). On the face with the normal \(\vek m\) the force acts obliquely, so also in shear, the square becomes a parallelogram, the angle at the corner is no longer right, and the fibre along \(\vek m\) also turns. The direction \(\vek m\) is a principal direction neither of stress nor of strain.

In this corollary we write the eigenvalues \(\sigma_1\) and \(\varepsilon_1\), not \(\lambda\), because in this section \(\lambda\) is a Lamé constant.

Corollary 3.20 Principal directions of stress and strain (glavne smeri napetosti in deformacije)

Let Hooke's law for an isotropic material hold (theorem 3.19) with \(\nu \neq -1\) and \(\nu \neq \tfrac12\), and let \(\vek n\) be a unit vector. If \(\vek n\) is a principal direction of stress, that is, \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \sigma_1\,\vek n\) for some number \(\sigma_1\), then \(\vek n\) is also a principal direction of strain, \(\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n = \varepsilon_1\,\vek n\) for some number \(\varepsilon_1\), and conversely.

Proof

We get both directions of the argument from the law written with matrices, because the identity matrix leaves every vector as it is.

  1. We write item 1 of the theorem with matrices:
    \[\ten\varepsilon = \frac{1 + \nu}{E}\,\ten\sigma - \frac{\nu}{E}\,(\tr\ten\sigma)\,\mat I .\]
    The entry \((x, x)\) of the right side is
    \[\frac{(1 + \nu)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \nu\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}})}{E} = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \nu\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}})}{E} ,\]
    which is the first equation of (3.27). The entry \((x, y)\) is \((1 + \nu)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}/E\), because \(\mat I\) has zeros off the diagonal. Likewise for the other entries.
  2. Let \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \sigma_1\,\vek n\). The product of a sum of matrices with a vector is the sum of the products (lemma 1.100), a multiple of a matrix is multiplied by a vector by taking the multiple out, and \(\mat I\,\vek n = \vek n\) (definition 1.108). Therefore
    \[\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n = \frac{1 + \nu}{E}\,\sigma_1\,\vek n - \frac{\nu}{E}\,(\tr\ten\sigma)\,\vek n = \frac{(1 + \nu)\,\sigma_1 - \nu\,\tr\ten\sigma}{E}\,\vek n ,\]
    and \(\vek n\) is a principal direction of strain. In figure 3.77 on the left, the first term lies on the line of \(\vek n\), because \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \sigma_1\,\vek n\), and the second term is a multiple of the vector \(\vek n\), because \(\mat I\,\vek n = \vek n\). Their sum \(\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n\) therefore stays on the line, in the figure \(1{,}3 - 0{,}36 = 0{,}94\) times the vector \(\vek n\).
  3. Let \(\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n = \varepsilon_1\,\vek n\). By item 2 of the theorem and the same rules, \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\vek n + 2\mu\,\varepsilon_1\,\vek n = (\lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} + 2\mu\,\varepsilon_1)\,\vek n\), and \(\vek n\) is a principal direction of stress.

Source: SADD §4.2 (PDF p. 94), where the result is Exercise 4.7. SADD adds that it also holds for some, but not all, anisotropic materials.

What happens for a direction that is not principal is shown in the right half of figure 3.77, for the direction \(\vek m\) of figure 3.76. The first term \(\tfrac{1 + \nu}{E}\,\ten\sigma\,\vek m\) points obliquely, because \(\ten\sigma\,\vek m\) is not a multiple of the vector \(\vek m\). The second term is a multiple of the vector \(\vek m\), so it only shifts the sum parallel to the line. The sum \(\ten\varepsilon\,\vek m\) therefore leaves the line, by the shear strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}}\), and the fibre along \(\vek m\) turns.

We have already seen this in pure shear. In the axes along the diagonals \(AC\) and \(BD\) in the proof of lemma 3.16 on strain in pure shear both matrices, \(\bar{\ten\sigma}\) and \(\bar{\ten\varepsilon}\), were diagonal, so the principal directions of stress and strain are the same: the directions of the two diagonals and the axis \(y\). In a plate with fibres pulled at a slant to the fibres, however, the tension also causes a shear strain between the direction of the tension and the direction perpendicular to it (CM, Fig. 6.3.4, PDF p. 268). The direction of the tension is a principal direction of stress, but not a principal direction of strain.

3.2.12 Where the law stops holding

The formulas (3.20) and (3.22) have \(1 - 2\nu\) and \(1 + \nu\) in their denominators. Figure 3.78 shows what happens when \(\nu\) approaches the two limits. On the horizontal axis is \(\nu\) from \(-1\) to \(0{,}5\), vertically are \(K/E\) and \(G/E\). For steel with \(\nu = 0{,}3\) the values are \(K/E = 0{,}833\) and \(G/E = 0{,}385\).

As \(\nu\) approaches \(0{,}5\), \(1 - 2\nu\) approaches zero, and the bulk modulus grows without bound (figure 3.78, blue curve). The volume of the material can hardly be compressed. Figure 3.79 shows the same on the relation \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = K\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\) of section 3.2.11, on the axes \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}/E\). Every \(\nu\) gives a line through the origin with the slope \(K/E\), flat at \(\nu = 0\), for steel with \(\nu = 0{,}3\) with the slope \(0{,}833\), at \(\nu = 0{,}45\) and \(0{,}49\) with the slopes \(3{,}33\) and \(16{,}7\). At \(\nu = 0{,}5\) the volumetric strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\) is zero under every stress, so the volume does not change up to terms that are products of strains, and the material is called incompressible (nestisljiv) (SADD, PDF p. 96, BOWER §3.2.6, PDF p. 102). Rubber has \(\nu = 0{,}49\) (BOWER, Table 3.1, PDF p. 100), and its bulk modulus is \(K = E/\big(3\,(1 - 2 \cdot 0{,}49)\big) = E/(3 \cdot 0{,}02) = 16{,}7\,E\). For an incompressible material item 2 of Hooke's law does not hold, since \(\lambda\) divides by \(1 - 2\nu = 0\) and is not defined (as \(\nu\) approaches \(0{,}5\) it grows without bound). The reason is physical: since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = 0\) under every stress, the line at \(\nu = 0{,}5\) is vertical, and the points \(A\) and \(B\) on it have the same \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = 0\) but different mean stresses. So we cannot compute the mean stress from the strains, the strain does not determine it. As \(\nu\) approaches \(-1\), on the other hand, the shear modulus grows without bound. Materials with negative \(\nu\) exist: a bar of such a material under tension gets thicker (BOWER, PDF p. 102), while a steel bar with \(\nu = 0{,}3\) gets thinner. In figure 3.80 the longitudinal strain of both bars is \(0{,}3\), the second bar has \(\nu = -0{,}3\), so the thickness \(h\) of both changes by \(0{,}3 \cdot 0{,}3\,h = 0{,}09\,h\), inwards for the steel bar, outwards for the other. For a stable material \(-1 < \nu < 0{,}5\) (BOWER, PDF p. 102). Why, we will show in section 3.6 with the work needed to deform a material.

We derived Hooke's law under the assumptions at the beginning of the section. Where one of them fails, the derivation does not hold, and the cases below show that the law does fail there.

  1. Above the yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) steel deforms permanently, the loading line breaks there. This happens at a strain of about \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}/E = 220\ \text{MPa}/196\ \text{GPa} = 0{,}00112\) (section 2.2).
  2. Rubber stays elastic even at large strains, but there the stress is no longer proportional to the strain (section 3.1). In figure 3.81, on the axes \(\varepsilon\) and \(\sigma\), the rubber curve keeps to the Hooke line at small strains, but at large strains it departs from it.
  3. For large rotations the small strain tensor no longer describes the changes of lengths, even if the material is elastic and the changes of lengths are small (BOWER §3.2.2, PDF p. 97). In figure 3.82 we only turn the piece by the angle \(\theta\) about the axis \(z\), and the edge has the same length after the turn as before. The point moves by the displacement \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = (\cos\theta - 1)\,x - \sin\theta\,y\), and by (1.59) \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \cos\theta - 1\), although none of the piece's lengths has changed. At \(\theta = 10^\circ\) this is \(-0{,}0152\), more than thirteen times the strain of steel at the yield stress, and the law would predict a stress that is not in the piece. At a turn \(\theta = 0{,}001\) rad (that is \(0{,}057^\circ\)), such as assumption 4 still allows, however, \(1 - \cos\theta = 5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\), only \(0{,}045\) % of the strain of steel at the yield stress. So assumption 4 bounds the rotations too, not only the strains.
  4. Crystals, wood and materials reinforced with fibres are not isotropic (SADD, PDF p. 92). They need more than two numbers, which we look at in section 3.4.
  5. When the temperature changes, a material expands even without stress. A steel bar heated by 30 K gets longer by \(4{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4}\) of its length, about as much as the plate above gets longer at 100 MPa.

We continue with the last assumption in the next section, where we extend Hooke's law to heated materials.
